objectives.statement: Select and correctly use a ruler or measuring cylinder to obtain a length or liquid volume, recording the result with an appropriate unit.
Describe how a clock, stopwatch or electronically triggered digital timer can be used to measure a time interval, and select a method suited to the interval being measured.
Determine the mean value of a small distance or short time by measuring several identical intervals together and dividing by their number, including finding the period of a pendulum.

theory_blocks.title: A measurement is a number with a unit
theory_blocks.body:
A statement such as ‘the table is 1.20’ is incomplete: it could mean metres, centimetres or another unit. A physical measurement combines [[blue:a numerical value with a unit]], for example $1.20\,\mathrm{m}$. The quantity being measured determines the instrument: a ruler measures a suitable length, a measuring cylinder measures liquid volume, and a clock or timer measures a time interval.

Before reading any instrument, first identify the numbered marks and calculate the value of one smallest division. Read only the precision supported by that scale. More written digits do not create more information. A useful measurement therefore answers four questions: what quantity is measured, which instrument is suitable, how the scale is read and which unit belongs to the result.

theory_blocks.title: Measuring length with a ruler
theory_blocks.body:
Place the ruler beside and parallel to the object. View the scale from directly above the mark being read so that the apparent position is not shifted by parallax. If the zero mark is intact, one end of the object may be aligned with it. If the end of the ruler is worn, place the object between two clear marks and calculate

$$\text{length}=\text{final scale reading}-\text{initial scale reading}.$$

For example, an object extending from $2.4\,\mathrm{cm}$ to $11.7\,\mathrm{cm}$ has length $11.7-2.4=9.3\,\mathrm{cm}$. Check by addition: $2.4+9.3=11.7$. This method measures the interval occupied by the object rather than assuming that the ruler edge represents zero.

assets.caption: A ruler whose first centimetre is worn away. The rod lies between the $2.4\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $11.7\,\mathrm{cm}$ marks, so its length is the interval $11.7-2.4=9.3\,\mathrm{cm}$; the eye is directly above the mark being read.
assets.purpose: Show that length is the interval between two intact scale marks, not the final reading, and that the line of sight must be perpendicular to the scale at the mark.

theory_blocks.title: Measuring liquid volume
theory_blocks.body:
A measuring cylinder is chosen according to the volume and precision needed. Place it upright on a level surface. Determine the value of one scale division, then bring your eye level with the liquid surface. Looking from above or below produces parallax.

Most common liquids form a concave meniscus: the surface is lower in the middle than at the sides. Read the scale at the bottom of this meniscus and include the scale unit, usually $\mathrm{cm^3}$ or mL. These units represent the same volume because $1\,\mathrm{mL}=1\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. Do not invent decimal places that the scale cannot support.

assets.caption: A measuring cylinder read at the bottom of the concave meniscus. The eye level with the surface gives the correct reading; looking from above gives a reading that is too high and looking from below one that is too low.
assets.purpose: Make the parallax error visible: the same meniscus appears at three different scale positions depending on where the eye is.

theory_blocks.title: Choosing a method for time
theory_blocks.body:
A time interval has a start event and a stop event. A wall clock may be suitable for an event lasting many minutes, and a hand-operated stopwatch may be suitable for a pendulum experiment lasting several seconds. Very short events may need a digital timer triggered electronically by a photogate, microphone or switch because human reaction time can be a large fraction of the interval.

A method description should name the timer, state exactly which event starts and stops it, give the unit and explain any repetition. The number of digits on a digital display does not by itself prove that the method is accurate: the triggering method and the experimental setup also matter.

theory_blocks.title: Measure a multiple, then find the mean
theory_blocks.body:
A single sheet may be too thin for a ruler, and one pendulum oscillation may be too short for reliable hand timing. Measure many identical intervals together so that the total is large enough to read, then divide by their number:

$$\text{mean small interval}=\frac{\text{measured total}}{\text{number of identical intervals}}.$$

For a pendulum, one complete oscillation returns the bob to its starting position while moving in the same direction. If it starts at the left side, one complete oscillation is left → centre → right → centre → left. If 20 complete oscillations take $32.0\,\mathrm{s}$, the period is

$$T=\frac{32.0\,\mathrm{s}}{20}=1.60\,\mathrm{s}.$$

The multiplication $20\times1.60\,\mathrm{s}=32.0\,\mathrm{s}$ checks the calculation. Timing many oscillations reduces the relative effect of pressing the stopwatch slightly early or late, but it does not remove a systematic error such as counting an incomplete cycle.

assets.caption: One complete oscillation of a pendulum released from the left: left → centre → right (stage 1) and right → centre → left (stage 2), returning the bob to its starting position moving in the same direction. The fiducial mark below the rest position fixes where the timing starts and stops.
assets.purpose: Define one complete oscillation visually, so that a count of 20 oscillations is a count of whole cycles and not of half swings.

keywords.definition: A property that can be measured and expressed as a numerical value with a unit.
The value represented by the interval between adjacent scale marks.
An apparent shift in a reading caused by viewing a scale from the wrong angle.
The curved surface of a liquid in a container.
The elapsed time between a defined start event and stop event.
One complete repeated motion that returns to the same position moving in the same direction.
The time taken for one complete oscillation.
A representative value found here by dividing a measured total by the number of equal intervals in that total.

worked_examples.statement: **A ruler with a damaged end.** A wooden block begins at the $1.8\,\mathrm{cm}$ mark and ends at the $13.2\,\mathrm{cm}$ mark. Find its length and explain why the two readings are used.
reasoning: The block does not start at the ruler's zero mark, so its length is not the final reading on its own: it is the interval the block actually spans on the scale.

That interval is found as final reading minus initial reading, because subtracting the initial reading removes whatever lies before the block, including a worn or damaged edge that would otherwise be mistaken for zero.
worked_examples.interpretation: $1.8\,\mathrm{cm}+11.4\,\mathrm{cm}=13.2\,\mathrm{cm}$, so the calculated interval returns the final reading.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reporting $13.2\,\mathrm{cm}$ as the length by assuming the block starts at the ruler's zero mark; this silently includes the $1.8\,\mathrm{cm}$ that lies before the block even begins.

worked_examples.statement: **Finding a pendulum period.** A student times 20 complete oscillations of a pendulum and records $32.4\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the period.
reasoning: The stopwatch display of $32.4\,\mathrm{s}$ is the total time for the whole set of 20 oscillations, not a direct reading of one, because a single hand-timed oscillation would be too short for reaction time to be a small part of it.

The period is defined as the mean time for one complete oscillation, so the total is divided by the number of oscillations: $T=t/N$. This also spreads the one start/stop reaction-time error over 20 cycles instead of repeating it 20 times.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Giving $32.4\,\mathrm{s}$ itself as the period, treating the total elapsed time for the whole set of oscillations as if it were the time for just one.

worked_examples.statement: **Measuring one thin sheet.** A stack of 200 identical sheets is $18.0\,\mathrm{mm}$ thick. Estimate the mean thickness of one sheet and explain why the stack is measured.
reasoning: One sheet alone would be far thinner than the smallest division a ruler can read with any confidence, so a single direct measurement of it would be mostly guesswork.
Measuring the whole stack turns an unreadably small thickness into a large, confidently readable one; the cost is that the reading is now the total for 200 sheets, not for one.
Dividing that total by the number of sheets shares it out evenly, which is a fair estimate because the sheets are identical, giving a mean thickness for one sheet.
worked_examples.solution: $\text{mean thickness}=\dfrac{18.0\,\mathrm{mm}}{200}=0.0900\,\mathrm{mm}$, reported as $0.090\,\mathrm{mm}$ given the precision of the measurement.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Trying to read one sheet directly with a ruler and reporting an invented value, instead of measuring the stack as a whole and dividing by the count.

guided_exercises.statement: A pencil lies between the $2.4\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $11.7\,\mathrm{cm}$ marks of a ruler. Calculate its length and state the unit.
common_errors: If you wrote $11.7\,\mathrm{cm}$, you reported a scale position rather than the interval occupied by the pencil.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Do not assume that the pencil starts at zero.

**Step 2 — Method:** Subtract the initial reading from the final reading.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $11.7-2.4=9.3\,\mathrm{cm}$. Check: $2.4+9.3=11.7$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check the answer by adding the length to the initial reading.

hints: The period is the mean time for one complete oscillation.
Use $T=t/N$.
Multiply your answer by 15 to check it.
guided_exercises.statement: A pendulum completes 15 oscillations in $24.6\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate its period.
common_errors: If your answer is $24.6\,\mathrm{s}$, you have not divided the measured total by the number of oscillations.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** The period is the mean time for one complete oscillation.

**Step 2 — Method:** Use $T=t/N$.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $T=24.6\,\mathrm{s}/15=1.64\,\mathrm{s}$. Check: $15\times1.64=24.6$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Multiply your answer by 15 to check it.

exam_questions.statement: A student investigates a pendulum using a small bob, string and stopwatch. Describe a method to determine the period of the pendulum as reliably as possible. Your answer should explain what counts as one oscillation and how the period is calculated.
exam_questions.answer: Displace the bob by a small amount and release it without pushing. Choose a fixed reference point. Start the stopwatch as the bob passes the reference point in a chosen direction. Count a suitable number of complete oscillations, such as 20; one complete oscillation returns the bob to the same position moving in the same direction. Stop the watch at the end of the final complete oscillation. Repeat the timing for the same number of oscillations and calculate a mean total time. Divide the mean total time by the number of oscillations to obtain the period in seconds.
mark_scheme: Uses a stopwatch or suitable timer and a pendulum with a small displacement.
Uses a fixed reference point and a consistent start/stop crossing.
Times several complete oscillations rather than one.
Defines or clearly describes one complete oscillation.
Repeats the measurement and finds a mean total time.
Calculates period = mean total time ÷ number of oscillations, with unit seconds.

exam_questions.statement:
The figure shows part of the scale of a measuring cylinder containing water.

(a) Determine the volume represented by one small division on this scale. [1]

(b) State the volume of water in the cylinder. [2]

(c) A student records the volume as $34.25\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. Explain why this is not an acceptable reading of this scale. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) The numbered marks at $20\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ and $30\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ are separated by five equal intervals, so one small division represents $10/5=2\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. (b) The bottom of the meniscus is level with the second small division above the $30\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ mark, so the volume is $30+2\times2=34\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. (c) The smallest division on the scale is $2\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, so the scale cannot support hundredths of a cubic centimetre; those digits have been invented rather than read.
mark_scheme: (a) Divides the $10\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ gap between numbered marks by its five equal intervals to obtain $2\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ per small division.
(b) Identifies the bottom of the meniscus as level with the second small division above the $30\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ mark.
(b) States the volume as $34\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, including the unit.
(c) States that the smallest division is $2\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, so digits beyond that precision are not supported by the instrument.

assets.caption: Part of a measuring cylinder scale, numbered every $10\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ with five equal intervals between numbered marks. The bottom of the meniscus is level with a small division above the $30\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ mark.
assets.purpose: Give the student an actual drawn scale with non-unit divisions to read, rather than a scale described in words.

exam_questions.statement:
A trolley takes about $0.25\,\mathrm{s}$ to travel between two marks on a track, and this time must be measured.

(a) State whether a hand-operated stopwatch or a digital timer triggered by two light gates is the better choice, and justify your answer. [2]

(b) State one detail of the method you have chosen that must be recorded if another student is to repeat the measurement. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) The digital timer triggered by two light gates. The timer is started and stopped electronically as the trolley passes each gate, so the experimenter's reaction time, which is of the order of $0.2\,\mathrm{s}$, does not enter the measurement; with a hand-operated stopwatch that reaction time would be a large fraction of a $0.25\,\mathrm{s}$ interval. (b) Any one of: the positions of the two gates on the track; which gate starts the timer and which stops it; the unit of the reading.
mark_scheme: (a) Chooses the digital timer triggered by light gates.
(a) Justifies the choice by comparing human reaction time with the $0.25\,\mathrm{s}$ interval, so that hand timing would change the result by a large fraction of it.
(b) Gives one reportable detail of the method, such as the positions of the gates, or which event starts and which stops the timer.

challenge_questions.statement: A student has only a metre rule with millimetre divisions and a hand-operated stopwatch whose display reads to $0.01\,\mathrm{s}$. (a) Timing one single oscillation of a pendulum gives $0.86\,\mathrm{s}$; timing 25 complete oscillations gives $20.5\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the period from the second measurement and explain why it is the more trustworthy of the two. (b) One sheet of paper is far too thin for the rule. A stack of 500 identical sheets is $48\,\mathrm{mm}$ thick; calculate the mean thickness of one sheet. (c) Explain why a display that reads to $0.01\,\mathrm{s}$ does not make a single hand-timed oscillation accurate to $0.01\,\mathrm{s}$.
hints: In both (a) and (b) the same rule applies: measure a large multiple, then divide by the number of identical intervals.
For (c), separate two different things: how finely the display can show a number, and how well the start and stop events are actually captured.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) $T=20.5\,\mathrm{s}/25=0.82\,\mathrm{s}$. Check: $25\times0.82\,\mathrm{s}=20.5\,\mathrm{s}$. It is more trustworthy because the single reaction-time error at the start and the single one at the stop are shared over 25 oscillations instead of falling on one. (b) $48\,\mathrm{mm}/500=0.096\,\mathrm{mm}$. Check: $500\times0.096\,\mathrm{mm}=48\,\mathrm{mm}$. (c) The display resolution only limits how finely a number can be shown; the measurement itself is limited by how accurately the student's hand starts and stops the watch, and that reaction time is of the order of $0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ — far larger than $0.01\,\mathrm{s}$ and a large fraction of one $0.82\,\mathrm{s}$ oscillation.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) $T=20.5\,\mathrm{s}/25=0.82\,\mathrm{s}$. Check: $25\times0.82\,\mathrm{s}=20.5\,\mathrm{s}$. It is more trustworthy because the single reaction-time error at the start and the single one at the stop are shared over 25 oscillations instead of falling on one. (b) $48\,\mathrm{mm}/500=0.096\,\mathrm{mm}$. Check: $500\times0.096\,\mathrm{mm}=48\,\mathrm{mm}$. (c) The display resolution only limits how finely a number can be shown; the measurement itself is limited by how accurately the student's hand starts and stops the watch, and that reaction time is of the order of $0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ — far larger than $0.01\,\mathrm{s}$ and a large fraction of one $0.82\,\mathrm{s}$ oscillation.
common_errors: Giving $20.5\,\mathrm{s}$ as the period, or multiplying by 25 instead of dividing.
Treating the number of digits on the display as a statement of how accurate the measurement is.

mcq.stem: Which method gives the most defensible reading of water volume in a measuring cylinder?
mcq.explanation: the upright cylinder, eye-level view and bottom of an ordinary concave meniscus avoid tilt and parallax errors.

flashcards.front: What two parts make a physical measurement complete?
flashcards.back: A numerical value and a unit, such as $7.3\,\mathrm{cm}$.

flashcards.front: How is an object's length found when it does not start at the ruler's zero mark?
flashcards.back: Subtract the initial scale reading from the final scale reading.

flashcards.front: How should the volume of water in a measuring cylinder be read?
flashcards.back: Keep the cylinder upright, place the eye level with the meniscus and read the bottom of the concave meniscus.

flashcards.front: What is one complete oscillation of a pendulum?
flashcards.back: A motion that returns the bob to the same position moving in the same direction; for example left → centre → right → centre → left.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between the time for several oscillations and the period?
flashcards.back: The total time is for all the timed oscillations; the period is the time for one complete oscillation: $T=\text{total time}/\text{number of complete oscillations}$, measured in seconds.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Writing more decimal places automatically makes a measurement more accurate.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners often confuse numerical detail with information actually supplied by the scale.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner invents extra digits beyond the smallest readable scale division.
misconceptions.correct_model: Record all information justified by the instrument scale. Extra unsupported digits do not improve the measurement.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask which mark on the instrument supplies each written digit, then remove any digit that cannot be read or reasonably estimated.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The time for several pendulum oscillations is the period of one oscillation.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The stopwatch displays one number, so the learner may attach that number directly to the requested quantity.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The total time is copied as the period without dividing by the number of complete oscillations.
misconceptions.correct_model: The period is the mean time for one complete oscillation: $T=t/N$.
misconceptions.remediation: Label the stopwatch value as total time for $N$ oscillations and check the calculated period by multiplying it by $N$.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The physical end of a ruler can always be treated as its zero mark.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Many classroom measurements begin by aligning an object with the ruler edge, so the distinction between edge and zero mark is hidden.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: When an object begins at a non-zero mark, the learner reports only the final reading.
misconceptions.correct_model: Length is the difference between the two scale readings. Starting away from zero also avoids a worn or damaged ruler edge.
misconceptions.remediation: Use an object placed between two non-zero marks and explicitly calculate final reading minus initial reading.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A liquid meniscus can be read accurately from any viewing angle.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The apparent position of the meniscus shifts only slightly, so parallax may go unnoticed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner views the cylinder from above or below or does not mention eye level in a method.
misconceptions.correct_model: Place the cylinder upright on a level surface and bring the eye level with the meniscus. For an ordinary concave liquid meniscus, read its bottom.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare eye-level and oblique views of the same cylinder and identify which view aligns the meniscus with the scale without parallax.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reporting the final ruler reading as the object's length when the object starts away from zero.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Calculate final reading minus initial reading.
common_mistakes.why: It's tempting to read off a single number from the ruler and treat it as the length, but that number is only correct if the object starts exactly at zero; otherwise it includes the gap before the object begins.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading a measuring cylinder from above or below.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Move the eye to the same level as the meniscus before reading the scale.
common_mistakes.why: Looking down or up at a curved liquid surface makes the meniscus appear higher or lower than it really is, an effect caused by the viewing angle (parallax error).

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating the total time for many oscillations as the period.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Divide the total time by the number of complete oscillations.
common_mistakes.why: The period is defined as the time for one oscillation, but it is easier and more accurate to time several at once, and that total can get mistaken for the final answer itself.

common_mistakes.mistake: Counting one-way motion from one side to the other as a complete oscillation.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: A complete oscillation returns to the starting position moving in the same direction.
common_mistakes.why: A swing from one side to the other looks like a complete back-and-forth motion, but the pendulum has only covered half of a full cycle; it still has to swing back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing extra decimal places unsupported by the scale.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Record only the precision that can be justified from the instrument.
common_mistakes.why: More decimal places can look more precise or more scientific, but a reading is only as precise as the smallest division the instrument can actually show.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving a measurement without a unit.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Attach the appropriate unit to every measured or calculated physical quantity.
common_mistakes.why: The numerical value on its own feels like the complete answer, but without a unit it is ambiguous or meaningless as a physical quantity.

exam_notes: In a practical-method question, name the instrument and describe how it is used; naming it alone is rarely sufficient.
State the eye position and the part of the meniscus read when describing liquid-volume measurement.
For a pendulum period, say that several complete oscillations are timed, the measurement is repeated and the mean total time is divided by the number of oscillations.
Always include a unit in the final answer and preserve sensible precision.

summary.core_message: Reliable measurement depends on a suitable instrument, correct scale reading, a stated unit and a method that matches the size of the interval.
key_points: Read a ruler from directly above and subtract two scale positions if the object does not start at zero.
Read an upright measuring cylinder at eye level and use the bottom of an ordinary concave meniscus.
Define start and stop events when measuring time, and use electronic triggering when an interval is too short for dependable hand timing.
For a small distance or short time, measure many identical intervals together and divide by their number.
The period is the mean time for one complete oscillation.

exit_check.question: Why is timing 20 pendulum oscillations usually better than timing one oscillation with a hand-operated stopwatch?
exit_check.answer: The total interval is longer, so the start/stop reaction-time error is a smaller fraction of the measured time. Dividing the total by 20 then gives the mean period.

summary.big_idea: Reliable measurement depends on a suitable instrument, correct scale reading, a stated unit and a method that matches the size of the interval.

02_Speed_velocity_and_the_role_of_direct.title: Speed, velocity and the role of direction
02_Speed_velocity_and_the_role_of_direct.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Define speed as distance travelled per unit time, use $v=s/t$, and calculate average speed from total distance travelled and total time taken, including any time spent stopped.
Distinguish a scalar quantity (magnitude only) from a vector quantity (magnitude and direction).
Classify every standard scalar and vector quantity, giving a reason based on whether a direction is needed to complete its description.
Define velocity as speed in a stated direction, and explain the distinction between distance travelled and displacement using an out-and-back journey.

prerequisites.statement: Measure or read off a distance and a time interval together with their correct units, as practised with rulers, cylinders and timers.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A speed calculation is only meaningful once both the distance and the time that go into it are genuine measured quantities with units attached.

prerequisites.statement: Divide one measured quantity by another and keep track of the resulting unit, for example finding how many metres correspond to one second of a journey.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every speed and velocity calculation in this lesson is a single division of a distance by a time. A learner who cannot form and simplify that ratio will get a wrong number even with a completely correct understanding of speed.

diagnostic_items.question: A cyclist covers $150\,\mathrm{m}$ in $30\,\mathrm{s}$ at a steady rate. What distance, in metres, does the ratio $150\div30$ represent for a single second?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $5\,\mathrm{m}$: dividing the total distance by the total time shares it evenly across every second, so $150\,\mathrm{m}\div30\,\mathrm{s}=5\,\mathrm{m}$ for each second.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner reports the time rather than carrying out the division, so the answer is not a distance for one second at all.
The learner multiplies the two numbers instead of dividing them.
The division is carried out correctly, but the unit of the answer is left as seconds instead of metres, showing that the ratio's meaning has not been tracked.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks the pure arithmetic skill of forming and simplifying a distance-over-time ratio before any physics vocabulary is attached to it.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write the relationship in words first — distance for one second = total distance ÷ total time — then repeat the calculation with two further pairs of numbers, stating the unit of the result each time before moving on to speed.

theory_blocks.title: From a measured distance to a description of motion
theory_blocks.body:
Lesson 1 produced numbers with units: a length in centimetres, a time in seconds. On their own, neither number describes motion. Put them together as a ratio — how much distance for how much time — and a new, more useful quantity appears: a measure of how quickly something is covering ground.

That ratio is [[blue:speed]]. It takes two measured quantities you already know how to obtain and combines them into one that tells a story a single length or a single time cannot: whether something is crawling or racing, and by how much more than another object.

theory_blocks.title: Average speed: $v=s/t$
theory_blocks.body:
Speed is distance travelled per unit time:

$$v=\frac{s}{t}$$

For a whole journey, **average speed uses the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken**, and that total time includes any time spent stopped. The common unit is $\mathrm{m/s}$; for a longer journey $\mathrm{km/h}$ may be more convenient.

For example, a learner travels $120\,\mathrm{m}$ in $20\,\mathrm{s}$: average speed $=120\,\mathrm{m}/20\,\mathrm{s}=6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Check by substitution: $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}\times20\,\mathrm{s}=120\,\mathrm{m}$.

Now suppose the same learner then stops for $10\,\mathrm{s}$ before completing a further $60\,\mathrm{m}$ in $10\,\mathrm{s}$. The average speed for the **whole** journey is not $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ any more:

$$\bar v=\frac{120\,\mathrm{m}+60\,\mathrm{m}}{20\,\mathrm{s}+10\,\mathrm{s}+10\,\mathrm{s}}=\frac{180\,\mathrm{m}}{40\,\mathrm{s}}=4.5\,\mathrm{m/s}.$$

Check: $4.5\,\mathrm{m/s}\times40\,\mathrm{s}=180\,\mathrm{m}$. The $10\,\mathrm{s}$ stop belongs in the total time even though no distance is added during it; leaving it out would wrongly give $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ again.

theory_blocks.title: An instant is not the whole journey
theory_blocks.body: A speedometer or a radar gun reports **instantaneous speed**: the speed at one particular moment. A journey's [[blue:**average speed**]] is a single number calculated afterwards from the total distance and the total time, and it does not have to match the speed at any one instant within that journey — in the example above, the learner's speed was $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ while moving and $0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ while stopped, and the average over the whole trip was $4.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$, a number that does not describe the speed during either moving leg.

theory_blocks.title: Scalars and vectors
theory_blocks.body:
A **scalar** quantity has magnitude only. A **vector** quantity has magnitude **and** direction, and a direction is part of what the quantity means — omitting it leaves the description incomplete, not merely less precise.

| Scalars (magnitude only) | Vectors (magnitude and direction) |
|---|---|
| distance | force |
| speed | weight |
| time | velocity |
| mass | acceleration |
| energy | gravitational field strength |
| temperature | |

A useful test: ask whether stating a direction changes what the quantity tells you about the situation. '$20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to the north' is meaningless, because a direction adds nothing to a temperature; '$20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to the north' is a genuinely different piece of information from '$20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to the south', because for a vector the direction is part of the answer.

theory_blocks.title: Velocity, displacement and the out-and-back journey
theory_blocks.body:
**Velocity** is speed in a stated direction: it is the vector partner of speed. **Displacement** is the vector partner of distance: it is the directed straight-line change from the starting position to the finishing position, not the length of the path actually followed.

An out-and-back journey makes the distinction impossible to miss. Suppose a walker covers $150\,\mathrm{m}$ east and then $50\,\mathrm{m}$ back west, in $100\,\mathrm{s}$ total. The **distance travelled** is $150\,\mathrm{m}+50\,\mathrm{m}=200\,\mathrm{m}$: every metre actually covered counts, regardless of direction. The **displacement** is the directed difference between the finish and the start: $150\,\mathrm{m}\text{ east}-50\,\mathrm{m}\text{ east}=100\,\mathrm{m}$ east — noticeably less than the distance travelled, because the return leg partly cancels the outward one. A walker who returned the full $150\,\mathrm{m}$ would have travelled $300\,\mathrm{m}$ but have a displacement of exactly zero, however long and tiring the walk.

Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time, and it is this cancellation that lets an object have a positive average speed and simultaneously a zero (or much smaller) average velocity for the same journey.

It is also worth noting now, ahead of the lessons that calculate it formally, that a moving object's velocity changes whenever its **direction** changes, even while its speed stays exactly the same — a car turning a corner at a constant reading on its speedometer is still changing velocity. That idea is picked up properly once acceleration is defined later in this unit.

keywords.definition: Distance travelled per unit time, $v=s/t$.
Total distance travelled divided by total time taken for a whole journey, including any time stopped.
The speed of an object at one particular moment, as a speedometer would show.
A quantity completely described by a magnitude alone.
A quantity that needs both a magnitude and a stated direction to be fully described.
The total length of the path actually followed by a moving object.
The directed straight-line change from an object's starting position to its finishing position.
Speed in a stated direction.

worked_examples.statement: **A straightforward speed calculation.** A runner covers $400\,\mathrm{m}$ in $50\,\mathrm{s}$ at a steady rate. Calculate the runner's speed.
reasoning: The runner moves at a steady rate, so a single ratio of the whole distance to the whole time correctly describes the motion throughout.
Speed is distance per unit time, so use $v=s/t$ directly with the two given values.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing the time by the distance instead of the distance by the time, which would give $0.125\,\mathrm{s/m}$ — a correct-looking number with the wrong meaning and the wrong unit.

worked_examples.statement: **A journey with a stop.** A delivery cyclist rides $120\,\mathrm{m}$ in $20\,\mathrm{s}$, stops for $10\,\mathrm{s}$ to check an address, then rides a further $60\,\mathrm{m}$ in $10\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the average speed for the whole trip.
unknowns: Average speed for the whole trip
reasoning: Average speed for a whole journey needs the total distance over the total time, not the speed of either moving leg on its own.
The $10\,\mathrm{s}$ stop adds no distance, but it is still part of the elapsed time of the trip and must be added into the total time.
Add the two distances and the three times separately before dividing, rather than averaging the two legs' individual speeds.
worked_examples.interpretation: $4.5\,\mathrm{m/s}\times40\,\mathrm{s}=180\,\mathrm{m}$, the correct total distance; note this is less than the $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ either moving leg achieved alone, because the stop is shared across the whole average.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Leaving the $10\,\mathrm{s}$ stop out of the total time and calculating $180\,\mathrm{m}/30\,\mathrm{s}=6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, which describes only the moving time, not the whole trip the question asks about.

worked_examples.statement: **Distance and displacement on a closed loop.** A cyclist rides one complete lap of a circular track of length $400\,\mathrm{m}$, taking $80\,\mathrm{s}$, and finishes exactly where she started. Find (a) her average speed and (b) her average velocity for the lap, and explain why the two answers are so different.
knowns: Start and finish positions are the same point
reasoning: Average speed only needs the total distance travelled, which is the full $400\,\mathrm{m}$ of the lap regardless of its shape.

Average velocity needs the displacement, the directed straight-line change from start to finish; because the lap finishes at the same point it started, that straight-line change is zero, however far the cyclist actually rode.
The two quantities are not approximations of each other: one measures path length, the other measures net directed change, and a closed loop is the case where they differ most starkly.
worked_examples.interpretation: A nonzero average speed together with a zero average velocity is not a contradiction: it is exactly what is expected whenever a journey returns to its starting point.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reporting the average velocity as $5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ as well, by quietly reusing the distance travelled as if it were the displacement.

worked_examples.statement: **A two-leg delivery flight.** A delivery drone flies $900\,\mathrm{m}$ due north in $300\,\mathrm{s}$, then $300\,\mathrm{m}$ due south in $100\,\mathrm{s}$ to avoid a tall building. Calculate (a) the drone's average speed and (b) its average velocity for the whole flight, giving a direction for (b).
reasoning: Average speed uses total distance, which adds the two legs' lengths regardless of their opposite directions: $900\,\mathrm{m}+300\,\mathrm{m}=1200\,\mathrm{m}$, over a total time of $300\,\mathrm{s}+100\,\mathrm{s}=400\,\mathrm{s}$.

Average velocity uses displacement, which treats north and south as opposite signs along one axis: taking north as positive, the net displacement is $900\,\mathrm{m}-300\,\mathrm{m}=600\,\mathrm{m}$ north, not the sum of the two leg lengths.
Divide each total by the same total time of $400\,\mathrm{s}$ to get the two averages, and attach the direction only to the velocity, never to the speed.
worked_examples.interpretation: The average speed ($3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$) is exactly double the average velocity's magnitude ($1.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$) here only because the return leg cancels exactly half of the outward displacement; this is a feature of these particular numbers, not a general rule linking the two quantities.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Adding $900\,\mathrm{m}$ and $300\,\mathrm{m}$ to find the displacement, instead of subtracting the southward leg from the northward one, because both legs are positive distances even though they point in opposite directions.

hints: Identify which quantity the question calls the distance and which it calls the time.
Use $v=s/t$ with those two values directly — there is no stop or change of direction to account for here.
Check your answer by multiplying it back by the time.
guided_exercises.statement: A walker covers $250\,\mathrm{m}$ in $50\,\mathrm{s}$ at a steady pace. Calculate the walker's speed.
common_errors: Writing the answer as $50\,\mathrm{m/s}$ by mixing up which number is the distance and which is the time.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Identify which quantity the question calls the distance and which it calls the time.

**Step 2 — Method:** Use $v=s/t$ with those two values directly — there is no stop or change of direction to account for here.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $v=250\,\mathrm{m}/50\,\mathrm{s}=5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Check: $5.0\times50=250$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your answer by multiplying it back by the time.

hints: List the total distance covered and the total time elapsed separately before dividing anything.
The delivery stop adds no distance, but it is still part of the total time of the trip.
Divide the total distance by the total time, not by the moving time alone.
guided_exercises.statement: A delivery van drives $40\,\mathrm{km}$ in $45$ minutes of actual driving, then stops for $15$ minutes to unload, making a total trip time of $1$ hour. Calculate the average speed for the whole trip in $\mathrm{km/h}$.
common_errors: Using the $45$ minutes of driving time instead of the full $1$ hour trip time, which would wrongly give $40\,\mathrm{km}/0.75\,\mathrm{h}\approx53\,\mathrm{km/h}$.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** List the total distance covered and the total time elapsed separately before dividing anything.

**Step 2 — Method:** The delivery stop adds no distance, but it is still part of the total time of the trip.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $\bar v=40\,\mathrm{km}/1\,\mathrm{h}=40\,\mathrm{km/h}$. Check: $40\times1=40$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Divide the total distance by the total time, not by the moving time alone.

exercises.statement: An athlete runs $800\,\mathrm{m}$ in a time of $2$ minutes $5$ seconds. Convert the time to seconds and calculate the athlete's average speed.
exercises.answer: $125\,\mathrm{s}$; $v=800\,\mathrm{m}/125\,\mathrm{s}=6.4\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
exercises.full_solution: $2$ minutes $5$ seconds $=120\,\mathrm{s}+5\,\mathrm{s}=125\,\mathrm{s}$. Then $v=800/125=6.4\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Check: $6.4\times125=800$.

exercises.statement: Classify each of the following as a scalar or a vector, giving a one-sentence reason: (a) the mass of a trolley, (b) the weight of the same trolley, (c) the time for an experiment, (d) the velocity of a falling ball, (e) the temperature of a room, (f) the gravitational field strength near Earth's surface.
exercises.answer: (a) scalar — mass has a size only. (b) vector — weight is a force and acts in a direction (downward). (c) scalar — time has a size only. (d) vector — velocity is speed with a stated direction. (e) scalar — temperature has a size only. (f) vector — gravitational field strength has a direction (toward the attracting mass).

exercises.statement: A shopper walks $150\,\mathrm{m}$ east along a mall corridor to a shop, then walks back $50\,\mathrm{m}$ west to a bench, taking $100\,\mathrm{s}$ in total. Calculate (a) the distance travelled, (b) the displacement from the starting point, (c) the average speed and (d) the average velocity.
exercises.answer: (a) $200\,\mathrm{m}$. (b) $100\,\mathrm{m}$ east. (c) $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (d) $1.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ east.
exercises.full_solution: Distance $=150+50=200\,\mathrm{m}$. Displacement (east positive) $=150-50=100\,\mathrm{m}$ east. Average speed $=200/100=2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Average velocity $=100/100=1.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ east.

exercises.statement: A factory conveyor belt carries a box $15\,\mathrm{m}$ in $25\,\mathrm{s}$, then halts for $10\,\mathrm{s}$ while an inspector checks it, then carries it a further $9\,\mathrm{m}$ in $15\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the average speed of the box for the whole process, and say which earlier example this calculation has the same structure as.
exercises.answer: $\bar v=(15\,\mathrm{m}+9\,\mathrm{m})/(25\,\mathrm{s}+10\,\mathrm{s}+15\,\mathrm{s})=24\,\mathrm{m}/50\,\mathrm{s}=0.48\,\mathrm{m/s}$; the structure is the same as the cyclist's journey with a stop.
exercises.full_solution: Total distance $=15+9=24\,\mathrm{m}$. Total time $=25+10+15=50\,\mathrm{s}$, including the $10\,\mathrm{s}$ inspection halt. $\bar v=24/50=0.48\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Check: $0.48\times50=24$. A conveyor belt that pauses is governed by exactly the same rule as a cyclist who stops: the halted time still belongs in the total.

exam_questions.statement: A hiker walks $5.0\,\mathrm{km}$ in the first hour, rests for $1.0$ hour, then walks a further $4.0\,\mathrm{km}$ in the next hour. (a) State the total distance walked. (b) State the total time taken. (c) Calculate the hiker's average speed for the whole walk, in $\mathrm{km/h}$.
mark_scheme: (a) $9.0\,\mathrm{km}$ (adds both walking legs, not the rest)
(b) $3.0\,\mathrm{h}$ (adds both walking hours and the resting hour)
(c) correct substitution of (a)/(b) regardless of their values
(c) $3.0\,\mathrm{km/h}$ with the unit stated

exam_questions.statement: A light aircraft flies $240\,\mathrm{km}$ due north in $1.0\,\mathrm{h}$, then turns and flies $90\,\mathrm{km}$ due south in a further $0.5\,\mathrm{h}$. (a) Calculate the total distance flown and the total time taken. (b) Calculate the average speed for the whole flight. (c) Calculate the resultant displacement from the starting point, stating a direction. (d) Calculate the average velocity for the whole flight, stating a direction.
mark_scheme: (a) distance $=240+90=330\,\mathrm{km}$
(b) $330/1.5=220\,\mathrm{km/h}$, unit required
(c) displacement found by subtraction (north taken as positive), not addition: $240-90=150\,\mathrm{km}$
(c) direction 'north' stated
(d) $150/1.5=100\,\mathrm{km/h}$ north, with direction stated

mcq.stem: A car's speedometer reads $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at one instant during a journey of $500\,\mathrm{m}$ that takes $50\,\mathrm{s}$ in total. What is the car's average speed for the whole journey?

options.why_wrong: this is the instantaneous speedometer reading at one moment, not the average over the whole $50\,\mathrm{s}$ journey.
this divides the distance by $20$, the speedometer reading, as though the journey lasted only $20\,\mathrm{s}$.
this divides the total time by the instantaneous reading instead of dividing the total distance by the total time.

mcq.explanation: Average speed uses total distance over total time: $500\,\mathrm{m}/50\,\mathrm{s}=10\,\mathrm{m/s}$, regardless of what any single instantaneous reading showed.

mcq.stem: A runner starts at a flag, runs $300\,\mathrm{m}$ around a closed track and finishes back at the same flag. What is the runner's displacement for this run?

options.why_wrong: this is the distance travelled around the track, not the directed change between the start and finish positions.
this halves the distance for no physical reason; the start and finish positions coincide exactly, not approximately.
this attaches a sign to the full distance instead of recognising that the straight-line change from start to finish is zero.

mcq.explanation: Displacement is the directed straight-line change from the starting position to the finishing position. Since the runner finishes exactly where she started, that change is zero, regardless of how far she actually ran.

mcq.stem: Which of these quantities is a vector?

options.text: the distance a car has travelled
options.why_wrong: distance is the total path length with no direction attached; it is a scalar.

options.text: the time taken for the journey
options.why_wrong: time has a size only and no direction; it is a scalar.
temperature has a size only; attaching a direction to it would add no information.

mcq.explanation: Velocity is speed in a stated direction, so it needs both a magnitude and a direction to be fully described; that is exactly what makes it a vector.

mcq.stem: A delivery van drives $20\,\mathrm{km}$ in $20$ minutes, stops for $10$ minutes to unload, then drives a further $10\,\mathrm{km}$ in $10$ minutes. What is the average speed for the whole trip, in $\mathrm{km/h}$?

options.why_wrong: this uses only the $30$ minutes of driving time and leaves the $10$-minute unloading stop out of the total time.
this divides only the first leg's $20\,\mathrm{km}$ by the full $40$-minute trip time, mixing one leg's distance with the whole trip's time.
this divides the distance in kilometres by the time in minutes without converting the time to hours.

mcq.explanation: Total distance $=20+10=30\,\mathrm{km}$. Total time $=20+10+10=40$ minutes $=\tfrac23\,\mathrm{h}$. Average speed $=30\div\tfrac23=45\,\mathrm{km/h}$.

flashcards.front: What is the equation for speed, and what does average speed use for a whole journey?
flashcards.back: $v=s/t$; average speed uses total distance divided by total time, including any time stopped.

flashcards.front: What makes a quantity a scalar?
flashcards.back: It is completely described by a magnitude alone; no direction is needed.

flashcards.front: What makes a quantity a vector?
flashcards.back: It needs both a magnitude and a stated direction; giving the magnitude alone leaves it incomplete.

flashcards.front: How do distance travelled and displacement differ?
flashcards.back: Distance is the total path length covered; displacement is the directed straight-line change from start to finish. They agree only for a one-way straight journey.

flashcards.front: A runner finishes a lap back at the start. Is her average velocity for the lap the same as her average speed?
flashcards.back: No. Average speed uses the full distance run around the lap, which is positive; average velocity uses displacement, which is zero because she returns exactly to her starting point.

flashcards.front: A journey includes a stop. Does the stopped time count toward the average speed calculation?
flashcards.back: Yes. The total time used in the average speed calculation includes every second that elapsed, moving or stopped.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The average speed of a whole journey is the same number as whatever a speedometer happens to read at some moment during it.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A speedometer gives one number at a time, so it feels natural to treat that single reading as a description of the whole trip, especially when the reading was taken somewhere in the middle of the journey.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner quotes an instantaneous reading given somewhere in the question as 'the average speed', without ever calculating total distance ÷ total time.
misconceptions.correct_model: Average speed is calculated only from the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken for the whole journey, and it generally differs from the speed at any one instant within that journey.
misconceptions.remediation: Give a journey where an instantaneous speed is stated and a different average speed can be calculated from the total distance and total time; ask the learner to identify which number the question that follows actually requires.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Distance travelled and displacement are always the same thing, just two different names for it.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: In a journey that goes straight from start to finish without changing direction, the path length and the straight-line separation do agree, so the difference is never noticed until a journey that returns toward its start is used.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner reports a nonzero displacement, or a nonzero average velocity, for a journey that finishes back at its starting point.
misconceptions.correct_model: Distance travelled is the total length of the path followed; displacement is the directed straight-line change from start position to finish position. The two agree only for a one-way straight journey, and displacement is zero for any journey that returns exactly to where it began, however far it actually travelled.
misconceptions.remediation: Work through an out-and-back journey step by step, calculating distance travelled and displacement separately and comparing the two results before calculating either speed or velocity.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Adding a direction to a measurement does not change what kind of quantity it is; distance and displacement, or speed and velocity, are just two ways of saying the same thing.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The paired words sound almost interchangeable in everyday speech and are measured with the same unit, so the difference in what information each one carries is easy to miss.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner treats a scalar and its paired vector as synonyms, or cannot say which of a list of named quantities needs a stated direction to be a complete description.
misconceptions.correct_model: A scalar is completely described by a magnitude alone. A vector additionally requires a stated direction, and a vector quantity given without its direction is an incomplete answer, not merely a 'rounded off' scalar.
misconceptions.remediation: Classify a mixed list of named quantities from the syllabus as scalar or vector, requiring a one-sentence reason for each that names whether direction is part of what the quantity means.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Time spent stopped during a journey can be left out of the total time used to calculate the average speed for the whole trip.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The object is not moving during the stop, so it feels as though that time contributes nothing to a description of how fast it moved.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: When calculating an average speed meant to describe an entire journey, the learner adds up only the moving segments' times and omits any stop.
misconceptions.correct_model: Average speed for a whole journey uses the total time that actually elapsed from start to finish, including any time spent stopped, because the average is being taken over the time that passed, not only over the time spent moving.
misconceptions.remediation: Recompute a stop-included average speed twice, once correctly with the stop included and once (deliberately) leaving it out, and compare the two results so the size of the error is visible.

common_mistakes.mistake: Quoting an instantaneous speed given somewhere in a question as if it were the journey's average speed.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Calculate average speed only from total distance divided by total time; never substitute a single reading for it.
common_mistakes.why: A single speed value mentioned partway through a question can look like it applies to the whole journey, but average speed depends on the total distance and total time, not on any one instant.

common_mistakes.mistake: Leaving a stop or rest out of the total time used for an average-speed calculation.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Add up every second that elapsed from the start of the journey to its end, moving or not, before dividing.
common_mistakes.why: A stop feels like 'nothing is happening', so it is easy to forget that time still passes and must be included in the total time of the journey.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating distance travelled and displacement as the same number for a journey that changes direction.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Calculate distance by adding every leg's length; calculate displacement by combining legs with their signs along a chosen positive direction.
common_mistakes.why: For a straight-line journey in one direction the two values happen to match, which can lead to assuming they are always interchangeable even when the journey doubles back.

common_mistakes.mistake: Giving a vector answer, such as a velocity, with no direction stated.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Treat the direction as part of the answer itself, not as an optional extra comment.
common_mistakes.why: The magnitude is often the part that takes the calculation, so the direction gets treated as an afterthought rather than as part of the answer itself.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming any two quantities measured in the same unit must be the same type of quantity.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask whether a direction changes the meaning of the quantity, not what unit it happens to share with another quantity.
common_mistakes.why: Sharing a unit feels like sharing a meaning, but the unit only describes the size of a quantity, not whether direction is part of its definition.

exam_notes: When a question gives a journey with a rest or a stop, always check whether the time asked for is the total trip time or only the moving time, and read off the total distance and total time from the question before substituting into $v=s/t$.
A displacement or a velocity answer is incomplete without a stated direction; state it explicitly, for example 'north', or give a sign after saying which direction is positive.
When a journey includes legs in opposite directions, find the displacement by combining the legs with signs along one chosen positive direction, not by adding their lengths as if they were distances.
If asked to justify that a quantity is a scalar or a vector, name explicitly whether a direction is needed to complete its description; do not simply assert the classification.

summary.big_idea: Speed turns a measured distance and a measured time into one useful ratio; adding a direction to distance and to speed turns them into displacement and velocity, which can tell a very different story from distance and speed alone.
key_points: Average speed is always total distance divided by total time, including any time stopped — never a single instantaneous reading.
A scalar needs a magnitude only; a vector needs a magnitude and a direction, and leaving the direction out leaves a vector incompletely described.
Distance travelled adds up every metre covered; displacement is the directed straight-line change from start to finish, and is zero for any journey that returns to its start.
Velocity is speed in a stated direction; average velocity is displacement divided by total time.
A journey can have a positive average speed and a zero (or much smaller) average velocity at the same time — this is expected, not contradictory, whenever the path changes direction.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Average speed uses total distance over total time, stop included; displacement is the directed shortcut from start to finish, not the path length, and it can be zero even after a long, fast journey.
