objectives.statement: Sketch, plot and interpret a distance–time graph with clearly labelled axes and units.
Identify rest, constant speed, speeding up and slowing down qualitatively from the shape of a distance–time graph.
Calculate speed from the gradient of a straight distance–time section, using two points taken from that same section, and check the resulting unit.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate average speed as total distance divided by total time, and recognise that the time used must include any time stopped.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: A graph's gradient is the same calculation drawn as a picture; the numerical rule learned in Lesson 2 is exactly what each gradient will compute.

prerequisites.statement: Read a pair of $(x,y)$-style coordinates from a set of labelled axes, and calculate a rise and a run between two marked points.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every gradient in this lesson is a rise (change in distance) divided by a run (change in time), read from two points on the same straight section. A learner who cannot read coordinates or subtract them correctly cannot get a correct speed, however well the physics is understood.

diagnostic_items.question: On a pair of axes, a straight line passes through the points $(2,5)$ and $(6,17)$. What is the rise (change in the vertical value) and the run (change in the horizontal value) between these two points?

common_wrong_answers.answer: Rise $=5$, run $=2$ (or similar: the raw coordinates, not the differences)
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner reports one point's coordinates instead of subtracting the two points to find the changes between them.
The learner adds the two vertical values and the two horizontal values instead of subtracting them.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Rise $=12$, run $=-4$ (or the signs swapped between rise and run)
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The subtraction is attempted but the two points are taken in a different order for the rise than for the run, scrambling the sign.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This isolates the pure coordinate-geometry skill — subtracting matching coordinates in a consistent order — that every gradient-as-speed calculation in this lesson depends on.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Practise finding the rise and run between two more pairs of points, always subtracting the earlier point's coordinates from the later point's coordinates in the same order for both the rise and the run, before any gradient is calculated.

theory_blocks.title: Turning a journey into a picture
theory_blocks.body:
Lesson 2 described a journey with numbers: distances, times, a calculated speed. A **distance–time graph** draws the same journey instead, with elapsed time along the horizontal axis and the total distance travelled so far along the vertical axis.

Every instant of the journey becomes one point on the page, and the whole journey becomes a line. Reading that line back is exactly the skill this lesson builds: a flat stretch, a rising stretch and a steep rising stretch are not just different shapes — each one is a different physical event, and [[blue:learning to read the shape is learning to read the motion]].

theory_blocks.title: The gradient of a straight section is the speed
theory_blocks.body:
On a **straight** section of a distance–time graph, speed equals the gradient:

$$\text{speed}=\frac{\Delta\text{distance}}{\Delta\text{time}}$$

Two points are needed, and both must lie on the **same** straight section. For example, if distance rises from $15\,\mathrm{m}$ at $3\,\mathrm{s}$ to $55\,\mathrm{m}$ at $8\,\mathrm{s}$ on one straight segment, the gradient is

$$\frac{55\,\mathrm{m}-15\,\mathrm{m}}{8\,\mathrm{s}-3\,\mathrm{s}}=\frac{40}{5}=8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}.$$

Check: at $8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for $5\,\mathrm{s}$, distance increases by $40\,\mathrm{m}$, which matches. The unit comes out as $\mathrm{m/s}$ automatically, because the vertical axis is in metres and the horizontal axis is in seconds — the unit is not chosen separately, it is forced by what each axis measures.

The table below plots one full journey; the matching graph, with its three labelled sections, is shown as the figure.

| Time (s) | 0 | 4 | 9 | 13 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Distance (m) | 0 | 12 | 12 | 52 |

assets.caption: A segmented distance–time graph matching the table: A rises at constant speed, B is a five-second rest at constant distance, and C rises faster than A over the same four-second span.
assets.purpose: Let the learner narrate rest and two different constant speeds directly from a single coherent journey, with the table and the graph reproducing exactly the same numbers.

theory_blocks.title: Reading the three sections
theory_blocks.body:
Using the figure: section **A** (0 s to 4 s) rises steadily from $0\,\mathrm{m}$ to $12\,\mathrm{m}$, a constant speed of $12/4=3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Section **B** (4 s to 9 s) stays flat at $12\,\mathrm{m}$: the object is at rest, speed $0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, for a full five seconds. Section **C** (9 s to 13 s) rises from $12\,\mathrm{m}$ to $52\,\mathrm{m}$, a constant speed of $(52-12)/4=10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ — steeper than A, and faster.

The contrast worth fixing: **height** on this graph tells you the total distance covered so far; **steepness (gradient)** tells you the speed during that section. Section C finishes at the greatest height **and** has the steepest slope, but those are two separate facts about it, not the same fact twice — a section can sit high up on the page and still be flat (a rest after a lot of earlier travel). Section B shows this: it sits at $12\,\mathrm{m}$, well above zero, yet its gradient is zero.

theory_blocks.title: Curves, and why two points must share a section
theory_blocks.body:
A **curved** section of a distance–time graph shows a continuously changing speed: a curve that gets steeper as it goes shows speeding up, and one that gets less steep shows slowing down. This unit does not require calculating a numerical gradient for a curve — reading the change in steepness qualitatively is enough at this stage.

What must never happen, on a straight or a curved graph, is [[red:picking two points from **different** sections and dividing their rise by their run as though that were a single speed]]. The result of such a calculation is a number, but it is not the speed of any real part of the motion: it is an average over a mixture of sections, including possibly a rest, that does not correspond to anything the object actually did at any one moment.

assets.caption: A distance–time graph with no straight section: the curve first gets steeper, so the object is speeding up, and then gets less steep, so it is slowing down. The dashed line marks the instant of greatest steepness, where the object is moving fastest.
assets.purpose: Give the curves paragraph the picture it describes, so that 'steepening' and 'flattening' are recognised as shapes rather than memorised as words.

keywords.definition: A graph with elapsed time on the horizontal axis and distance travelled on the vertical axis.
The rise divided by the run between two points on a straight section of a graph.
A state in which distance travelled is not changing; shown as a horizontal section with gradient zero.
A part of a graph over which the gradient does not change, representing constant speed.
A part of a graph over which the gradient itself changes, representing a continuously changing speed.

worked_examples.statement: **A single straight section.** On a straight section of a distance–time graph, distance rises from $15\,\mathrm{m}$ at $t=3\,\mathrm{s}$ to $55\,\mathrm{m}$ at $t=8\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the speed during this section.
knowns: Both points lie on the same straight section
reasoning: Because the section is straight, its gradient is constant throughout, so any two points taken from it give the same speed.
Subtract the two distance readings for the rise and the two time readings for the run, keeping the later point first in both subtractions so the signs stay consistent.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check by substitution: at $8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for $5\,\mathrm{s}$, distance increases by $40\,\mathrm{m}$, taking it from $15\,\mathrm{m}$ to $55\,\mathrm{m}$ — exactly as given.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Subtracting $3\,\mathrm{s}$ from $15\,\mathrm{m}$ or otherwise mixing which number belongs to which axis, instead of subtracting distance from distance and time from time separately.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading the three-section journey.** Using the figure above (the table $t=0,4,9,13\,\mathrm{s}$ with distance $0,12,12,52\,\mathrm{m}$), describe what is happening in section B and calculate the speed there.
knowns: Distance is $12\,\mathrm{m}$ at both ends of section B
reasoning: The distance coordinate does not change across section B: it is $12\,\mathrm{m}$ at the start and $12\,\mathrm{m}$ at the end.
A speed is a rate of change of distance; if the distance is not changing while five seconds pass, that rate of change is exactly zero, so the object is at rest.
worked_examples.solution: $\text{speed}=\dfrac{12\,\mathrm{m}-12\,\mathrm{m}}{9\,\mathrm{s}-4\,\mathrm{s}}=\dfrac{0\,\mathrm{m}}{5\,\mathrm{s}}=0\,\mathrm{m/s}$: the object is at rest for the whole five seconds.
worked_examples.interpretation: The object's distance coordinate, $12\,\mathrm{m}$, is far from zero — it has already travelled a long way — but that large height is not the same fact as its speed, which is zero throughout this section.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Describing section B as 'moving slowly' rather than 'at rest', because the line is not at the very bottom of the graph.

worked_examples.statement: **Height versus steepness.** At $t=13\,\mathrm{s}$, the object in the figure has reached $52\,\mathrm{m}$, its greatest distance so far, and section C (the final section) is also the steepest of the three. Explain whether these two facts — greatest height and steepest slope occurring together — must always happen together on any distance–time graph.
unknowns: Whether greatest height and steepest section are logically linked
reasoning: Height at any instant reports total distance travelled up to that instant; it can only ever increase or stay level, so the final point of a graph is always its highest point by definition, independent of how steep any one section was.
Steepness reports the local speed of just one section, which can be large or small (or zero, as in section B) regardless of how high up the graph it happens to sit.

The two facts coincided here only because the final section, C, happened to be chosen as the fastest one; a graph could just as easily have its steepest section first and a slow or resting section last, still finishing at the greatest height by definition.
worked_examples.solution: No: a graph's final point is always its greatest height by definition, but the final section does not have to be the steepest one. The two facts coinciding in this figure is a feature of this particular journey, not a general rule.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is exactly the reasoning that the related idea gets backwards when comparing two different travellers rather than two sections of one graph: height answers 'how far so far', steepness answers 'how fast right now', and neither determines the other.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Arguing that the steepest section must always be the last one because 'that's where the graph is highest', confusing the two separate readings again.

worked_examples.statement: **A decoy point.** A distance–time table reads $t=0,3,6,9\,\mathrm{s}$ with distance $8,8,8,32\,\mathrm{m}$. A student calculates speed using the points $(0\,\mathrm{s},\,8\,\mathrm{m})$ and $(9\,\mathrm{s},\,32\,\mathrm{m})$. Show that this gives a different number from the gradient of the actual rising section, and explain why the student's number has no direct physical meaning.
knowns: Rest section: $t=0$ to $6\,\mathrm{s}$, distance fixed at $8\,\mathrm{m}$
Rising section: $t=6\,\mathrm{s}$ to $9\,\mathrm{s}$, distance rises from $8\,\mathrm{m}$ to $32\,\mathrm{m}$
unknowns: The correct speed of the rising section
reasoning: The actual rising section runs only from $t=6\,\mathrm{s}$ to $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$; its gradient uses only the two points at the ends of that section.

The student's two points, at $t=0\,\mathrm{s}$ and $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$, straddle both the rest section and the rising section, so the result mixes six seconds of standing still into what is supposed to describe the rising motion alone.
Comparing the two results numerically shows they disagree, which is itself the proof that the student's pairing does not isolate a single real speed.
worked_examples.solution: Correct gradient of the rising section: $\dfrac{32\,\mathrm{m}-8\,\mathrm{m}}{9\,\mathrm{s}-6\,\mathrm{s}}=\dfrac{24}{3}=8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The student's calculation: $\dfrac{32\,\mathrm{m}-8\,\mathrm{m}}{9\,\mathrm{s}-0\,\mathrm{s}}=\dfrac{24}{9}\approx2.7\,\mathrm{m/s}$, a different number that describes neither the rest nor the rise on its own.
worked_examples.interpretation: $2.7\,\mathrm{m/s}$ is not wrong arithmetic — it is a correctly computed answer to a question nobody asked: it averages six seconds of rest into three seconds of genuine motion, which is why it is smaller than the true $8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ of the rising section.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Picking the first and last points of a table as 'the two points' for a gradient calculation by habit, without first checking that a single straight section actually joins them.

hints: Identify the rise (change in distance) and the run (change in time) between the two given points.
Divide the rise by the run; do not divide the run by the rise.
Check your unit: metres divided by seconds must give metres per second.
guided_exercises.statement: A single straight section of a distance–time graph passes from $0\,\mathrm{m}$ at $t=0\,\mathrm{s}$ to $35\,\mathrm{m}$ at $t=5\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the speed during this section.
common_errors: Writing the answer as $5/35\,\mathrm{s/m}$, which inverts both the ratio and the unit.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Identify the rise (change in distance) and the run (change in time) between the two given points.

**Step 2 — Method:** Divide the rise by the run; do not divide the run by the rise.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $\text{speed}=35\,\mathrm{m}/5\,\mathrm{s}=7.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your unit: metres divided by seconds must give metres per second.

hints: Plot or picture the three points in order and identify which pairs lie on the same straight section.
There is one rising section, one rest, and one further rising section; treat each separately.
Calculate the second rising section's gradient using only its own two endpoints.
guided_exercises.statement: A distance–time table reads $t=0,4,8,12\,\mathrm{s}$ with distance $0,20,20,44\,\mathrm{m}$. (a) Describe what is happening between $t=4\,\mathrm{s}$ and $t=8\,\mathrm{s}$. (b) Calculate the speed of the final section, from $t=8\,\mathrm{s}$ to $t=12\,\mathrm{s}$.
guided_exercises.answer: (a) The object is at rest: distance stays at $20\,\mathrm{m}$ for the whole four seconds. (b) $(44-20)/(12-8)=24/4=6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
common_errors: Using $t=0\,\mathrm{s}$ and $t=12\,\mathrm{s}$ for part (b), which mixes the first rising section and the rest into the final section's gradient (the related idea).
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Plot or picture the three points in order and identify which pairs lie on the same straight section.

**Step 2 — Method:** There is one rising section, one rest, and one further rising section; treat each separately.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** (a) The object is at rest: distance stays at $20\,\mathrm{m}$ for the whole four seconds. (b) $(44-20)/(12-8)=24/4=6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Calculate the second rising section's gradient using only its own two endpoints.

exercises.statement: A straight section of a distance–time graph passes through the points $(2\,\mathrm{s},\,8\,\mathrm{m})$ and $(6\,\mathrm{s},\,28\,\mathrm{m})$. Calculate the speed during this section, with its unit.
exercises.full_solution: Rise $=28-8=20\,\mathrm{m}$; run $=6-2=4\,\mathrm{s}$; speed $=20/4=5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Check: $5.0\times4=20$.

exercises.statement: A cyclist's distance–time graph has four sections, in order: resting, rising steadily, rising more steeply than the previous section, then resting again. For each of the four sections, state whether the cyclist is at rest, moving at constant speed, or changing speed, and state which of the two moving sections is the faster one and how you can tell from the graph alone.
exercises.answer: Section 1: at rest. Section 2: constant speed. Section 3: constant speed, faster than section 2. Section 4: at rest. Section 3 is faster because it is steeper (a greater gradient), not because the graph happens to be higher up by that point.

exercises.statement: Two travellers are compared over a ten-second interval. Traveller A moves at a steady speed for the whole interval, covering $40\,\mathrm{m}$ in total. Traveller B covers $16\,\mathrm{m}$ in the first eight seconds at a steady rate, then sprints the final two seconds, covering a further $20\,\mathrm{m}$ in that short burst. (a) Calculate Traveller A's constant speed. (b) Calculate Traveller B's speed during the first eight seconds and during the final sprint. (c) At $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$, which traveller is moving faster, even though Traveller B has covered less total distance than Traveller A? Explain using gradients, not heights.
exercises.answer: (a) $40/10=4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (b) First part: $16/8=2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$; sprint: $20/2=10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (c) Traveller B, because at $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$ B is sprinting at $10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, a steeper local gradient than A's constant $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, even though B's total distance so far ($16\,\mathrm{m}+\text{part of the sprint}$) is less than A's.
exercises.full_solution: (a) $v_A=40/10=4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (b) $v_{B1}=16/8=2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$; $v_{B2}=(16+20-16)/(10-8)=20/2=10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (c) Speed at an instant is read from the local gradient, not from which graph is higher. At $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$, B's gradient is $10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, steeper than A's $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so B is moving faster at that instant despite trailing A on total distance.

exercises.statement: A water tank is filled at a steady rate. A height–time graph for the tank rises in a straight line from $0\,\mathrm{cm}$ at $t=0$ to $18\,\mathrm{cm}$ at $t=6$ minutes. Calculate the filling rate in $\mathrm{cm/min}$, and explain why this calculation uses exactly the same reasoning as a distance–time gradient, even though nothing here is actually travelling anywhere.
exercises.answer: Filling rate $=18\,\mathrm{cm}/6\,\mathrm{min}=3.0\,\mathrm{cm/min}$. The reasoning is identical to a distance–time gradient because both calculations find how much one quantity (distance, or here, height) changes per unit of another (time); the gradient rule does not require the changing quantity to be a position in space.
exercises.full_solution: Rise $=18\,\mathrm{cm}$, run $=6\,\mathrm{min}$, so the gradient is $18/6=3.0\,\mathrm{cm/min}$. Check: $3.0\times6=18$. A distance–time gradient and this height–time gradient are the same mathematical operation applied to two different physical quantities; 'gradient = rate of change' is the general idea, and speed is only its best-known example.

exercises.statement: The figure shows the distance–time graph of a cyclist, in three sections A, B and C. (a) Calculate the speed during section A, showing the two points you read from the graph. (b) Describe what is happening in section B and state how the shape of the graph tells you this. (c) State what section C shows. (d) Explain why the gradient method cannot give one single speed for section B.
exercises.answer: (a) Section A is straight from $(0\,\mathrm{s},\,0\,\mathrm{m})$ to $(4\,\mathrm{s},\,16\,\mathrm{m})$, so the speed is $(16-0)/(4-0)=4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (b) The cyclist is slowing down: the curve keeps rising, so the distance travelled is still increasing, but it becomes less and less steep, so each second adds less distance than the one before. (c) Section C is horizontal at $32\,\mathrm{m}$, so the cyclist is at rest, having travelled $32\,\mathrm{m}$ in total. (d) A gradient needs two points on one straight section. Section B is curved, so its steepness is different at every instant; any two points chosen on it would give an average over the whole curved stretch, not the speed at any one moment.
exercises.full_solution: Check for (a): at $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for $4\,\mathrm{s}$ the distance increases by $16\,\mathrm{m}$, which is the height of the graph at $t=4\,\mathrm{s}$.

assets.caption: A cyclist's distance–time graph: section A is a straight rise, section B is a curve that flattens out, and section C is horizontal.
assets.purpose: Make the student read a straight gradient and a curved section off a drawn, gridded graph rather than from a verbal description.

exercises.statement:
A runner's distance from the start is recorded every two seconds.

| Time (s) | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Distance (m) | 0 | 9 | 18 | 18 | 18 | 33 |

(a) Plot these points on graph paper, choosing scales that use at least half of the grid in each direction, labelling each axis with its quantity and unit, and joining the points with straight lines. (b) Describe the three sections of the journey. (c) Calculate the speed of the first section and of the last section.
exercises.answer: (a) Time on the horizontal axis from $0$ to $10\,\mathrm{s}$ and distance on the vertical axis from $0$ to $33\,\mathrm{m}$ (for example $35\,\mathrm{m}$ full scale), both axes labelled 'time (s)' and 'distance (m)'; the six points are joined by straight lines. (b) From $0$ to $4\,\mathrm{s}$ the runner moves at a constant speed; from $4\,\mathrm{s}$ to $8\,\mathrm{s}$ the graph is horizontal at $18\,\mathrm{m}$, so the runner is at rest; from $8\,\mathrm{s}$ to $10\,\mathrm{s}$ the graph rises more steeply than at the start, so the runner moves at a greater constant speed. (c) First section: $(18-0)/(4-0)=4.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Last section: $(33-18)/(10-8)=7.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: at $4.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for $4\,\mathrm{s}$ the runner covers $18\,\mathrm{m}$, and at $7.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for $2\,\mathrm{s}$ a further $15\,\mathrm{m}$, giving $18+15=33\,\mathrm{m}$ in total, which matches the table. Note that the point at $t=2\,\mathrm{s}$, $9\,\mathrm{m}$ lies on the same straight line, confirming that the first section really is at one constant speed.

exam_questions.statement: A distance–time table reads $t=0,3,6,9\,\mathrm{s}$ with distance $8,8,8,32\,\mathrm{m}$. (a) State which section of the journey is a rest, giving the time interval. [1] (b) Calculate the speed of the rising section only, showing which two points you used. [3]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Rest from $t=0\,\mathrm{s}$ to $t=6\,\mathrm{s}$, where distance stays at $8\,\mathrm{m}$. (b) Using $(6\,\mathrm{s},8\,\mathrm{m})$ and $(9\,\mathrm{s},32\,\mathrm{m})$: $(32-8)/(9-6)=24/3=8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
mark_scheme: (a) correct interval $t=0$ to $6\,\mathrm{s}$ identified as rest
(b) correct two points chosen, both on the rising section ($t=6\,\mathrm{s}$ and $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$)
(b) correct substitution $24/3$
(b) $8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ with unit stated

exam_questions.statement: A distance–time graph has three sections: from $t=0$ to $4\,\mathrm{s}$, distance rises from $0\,\mathrm{m}$ to $24\,\mathrm{m}$; from $t=4\,\mathrm{s}$ to $7\,\mathrm{s}$, distance stays at $24\,\mathrm{m}$; from $t=7\,\mathrm{s}$ to $9\,\mathrm{s}$, distance rises from $24\,\mathrm{m}$ to $40\,\mathrm{m}$. (a) Describe, in words, what is happening in each of the three sections. [3] (b) Calculate the speed in the first section and in the third section, and state which one is faster. [3]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Section 1: constant speed, moving. Section 2: at rest. Section 3: constant speed, moving, faster than section 1. (b) Section 1: $24/4=6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$; section 3: $(40-24)/(9-7)=16/2=8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$; section 3 is faster.
mark_scheme: (a) section 1 correctly described as constant speed
(a) section 2 correctly described as at rest
(a) section 3 correctly described as constant speed, faster than section 1
(b) section 1 speed $6.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ correctly calculated
(b) section 3 speed $8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ correctly calculated, using only its own two endpoints
(b) correct comparison stated (section 3 faster)

exam_questions.statement:
The figure shows the distance–time graph of a cyclist.

(a) State the time interval during which the cyclist is at rest. [1]

(b) Using two points read from the graph, calculate the speed during the first section. [2]

(c) Calculate the speed during the final section and state which of the two moving sections is the faster. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) The graph is horizontal from $t=5\,\mathrm{s}$ to $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$, so the cyclist is at rest for those $4\,\mathrm{s}$. (b) Reading $(0\,\mathrm{s},\,0\,\mathrm{m})$ and $(5\,\mathrm{s},\,20\,\mathrm{m})$ from the first section: speed $=(20-0)/(5-0)=4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (c) Reading $(9\,\mathrm{s},\,20\,\mathrm{m})$ and $(15\,\mathrm{s},\,50\,\mathrm{m})$: speed $=(50-20)/(15-9)=30/6=5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The final section is the faster, which agrees with it being the steeper of the two rising sections.
mark_scheme: (a) States the rest interval as $t=5\,\mathrm{s}$ to $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$.
(b) Reads two points from the first straight section, such as $(0,0)$ and $(5,20)$.
(b) Calculates $20/5=4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, with the unit.
(c) Calculates $(50-20)/(15-9)=5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, with the unit.
(c) States that the final section is the faster, justified by its greater steepness or by the two calculated values.

assets.caption: A cyclist's distance–time graph on a numbered grid: a straight rise, a horizontal section, then a steeper straight rise.
assets.purpose: Give an exam question in which the values must be read off a drawn, gridded graph, as in a real IGCSE paper.

mcq.stem: A car drives around a gentle bend. Its distance–time graph for this part of the journey is a single straight rising line. What can be concluded from this graph?

options.text: The road itself must be straight at this point
options.why_wrong: the graph plots distance travelled against time, not the geometric shape of the road; a car can produce a straight distance-time line while following a curved road, as long as its speed stays constant.

options.text: No conclusion about the car's speed can be drawn from a straight line
options.why_wrong: a straight distance-time line is exactly the signature of constant speed; it is the most direct conclusion the graph supports.
a stationary car produces a horizontal line, not a rising one; this graph is rising throughout.

options.text: The car is travelling at a constant speed

mcq.explanation: A straight rising distance–time line means equal distances are covered in equal times, which is the definition of constant speed — it says nothing about the geometric shape of the road being followed.

mcq.stem: A distance–time graph has a horizontal section lasting several seconds. What can be concluded about the object's speed during this section?

options.text: It is zero: the object is at rest
It is a constant, nonzero speed
options.why_wrong: a horizontal section means the distance coordinate is not changing at all, which rules out any nonzero speed.

options.text: It is at its maximum value for the whole journey
options.why_wrong: nothing about a flat section implies maximum speed; in fact the opposite is true, since the speed here is the smallest possible value, zero.

options.text: It cannot be found without more information
options.why_wrong: the gradient of a horizontal section is always exactly zero, which is already enough information to find the speed.

mcq.explanation: A horizontal section has $\Delta\text{distance}=0$ over a nonzero $\Delta\text{time}$, so its gradient — and therefore its speed — is exactly zero: the object is at rest.

mcq.stem: At $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$, Traveller A has covered $36\,\mathrm{m}$ in total and is moving at a steady $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Traveller B has covered only $16\,\mathrm{m}$ in total but is, at this exact instant, in the middle of a brief sprint at $10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Which traveller is moving faster at this instant?

options.text: Traveller A, because A's graph is higher up at this instant
options.why_wrong: A's larger total distance shows A is ahead overall, not that A is faster right now; speed at an instant is read from the gradient, not the height.

options.text: Both are moving at the same speed at this instant
options.why_wrong: the two stated instantaneous speeds, $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, are different numbers, not equal ones.

options.text: It cannot be determined without seeing the full shape of both graphs
options.why_wrong: both instantaneous speeds are already given directly in the question; no further graph shape is needed to compare them.

mcq.explanation: Speed at an instant is the local gradient, not the total distance covered so far. Traveller B's $10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at this instant is steeper than Traveller A's steady $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, even though B is behind on total distance.

mcq.stem: A distance–time table reads $t=0,4,9,13\,\mathrm{s}$ with distance $0,12,12,52\,\mathrm{m}$, with a rest between $t=4\,\mathrm{s}$ and $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$. Which calculation correctly finds the speed of the final rising section, from $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$ to $t=13\,\mathrm{s}$?

options.text: $(52-0)/(13-0)=4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, using the very first and very last points
options.why_wrong: this spans the whole journey, including the rising first section and the five-second rest, so it does not isolate the final section's own gradient.

options.text: $(12-12)/(9-4)=0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, using the two points at the ends of the rest
options.why_wrong: this correctly calculates zero, but zero is the speed of the rest section (B), not of the final rising section (C) the question asks about.

options.text: $(52-12)/(13-9)=10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, using the two points at the ends of the final section
$(12-0)/(4-0)=3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, using the two points at the ends of the first section
options.why_wrong: this correctly calculates the first rising section's speed, not the final section's; the two points chosen do not lie on the final section at all.

mcq.explanation: The final rising section runs only from $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$ ($12\,\mathrm{m}$) to $t=13\,\mathrm{s}$ ($52\,\mathrm{m}$); using exactly those two points gives $(52-12)/(13-9)=10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Every other option uses at least one point from a different section.

flashcards.front: What goes on each axis of a distance–time graph, and what does a straight rising section's gradient equal?
flashcards.back: Time on the horizontal axis, distance travelled on the vertical axis; the gradient of a straight rising section equals the speed during it.

flashcards.front: A distance–time graph has a horizontal section well above zero on the distance axis. Is the object moving quickly, slowly, or not at all?
flashcards.back: Not at all: a horizontal section always means rest (speed zero), no matter how large its distance coordinate is.

flashcards.front: On a distance–time graph, what does height tell you and what does steepness tell you?
flashcards.back: Height tells you the total distance travelled so far; steepness (gradient) tells you the speed at that point. One does not determine the other.

flashcards.front: To find the speed of one section of a distance–time graph, which two points should you use?
flashcards.back: Two points that both lie on that same straight section — never one point from a different section or from either side of a rest.

flashcards.front: A car drives around a curved road at constant speed. What shape is its distance–time graph?
flashcards.back: A straight rising line: the graph's shape records how distance changes with time, not the geometric shape of the road.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The line drawn on a distance–time graph is a picture of the physical path the object actually followed through space.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both the graph and a real journey can be drawn as lines, so the drawn line is mistaken for a map rather than a record of one quantity (distance) changing against another (time).
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a straight rising graph line as meaning the object 'travelled in a straight line', or expects a graph for a journey around a bend to itself bend.
misconceptions.correct_model: A distance–time graph plots distance travelled against elapsed time; its shape describes how that distance changes over time, and says nothing directly about the geometric shape of the path taken. A car driving in a circle at constant speed produces a straight rising distance–time line, not a circular one.
misconceptions.remediation: Contrast a real curved path (for example a car going round a bend at constant speed) with the straight rising distance–time graph it actually produces, and ask what the graph's straightness is really telling us (that the speed is constant, not that the road is straight).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A horizontal section of a distance–time graph means the object is moving at some constant, nonzero speed.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A horizontal line still looks like 'a line going somewhere' on the page, and learners who associate any straight section with 'moving steadily' overgeneralise the rule from the rising sections to the flat one.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner calculates a nonzero gradient for a horizontal section, or describes it in words as 'constant speed' instead of 'at rest'.
misconceptions.correct_model: A horizontal section means the distance travelled is not changing while time passes, so the object's speed during that interval is exactly zero: it is at rest, however large its distance coordinate happens to be.
misconceptions.remediation: Calculate the gradient of a horizontal section explicitly ($\Delta\text{distance}=0$, so gradient $=0$) and connect that zero value in words to 'at rest', rather than leaving 'horizontal' and 'rest' as two separate facts to memorise.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Whichever traveller's graph is drawn higher up at a given time must necessarily be moving faster at that instant.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Height on the page is the most visually obvious feature of the graph, so it is mistaken for speed, which is actually shown by steepness (gradient), not height.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: When comparing two travellers' graphs, the learner identifies the one with the larger distance coordinate at a chosen time as 'the faster one', without checking either graph's gradient at that instant.
misconceptions.correct_model: Height on a distance–time graph shows how far an object has travelled in total so far; speed at an instant is shown by the steepness of the graph at that instant, not by how high up the graph currently is. A traveller who is behind overall can still be moving faster right now.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare two travellers at one chosen instant where the one with the smaller total distance has the steeper local gradient, and show explicitly that steepness, not height, answers 'who is faster right now'.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Any two labelled points on a distance–time graph can be used to calculate 'the' gradient, regardless of whether they lie on the same straight section.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Once the rule 'gradient $=\Delta$distance$/\Delta$time' is learned as a pure arithmetic recipe, it is applied to whichever two points are easiest to read off, without first checking that a single straight section actually joins them.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's chosen pair of points spans a rest section, or spans two sections with different gradients, and so computes a number that does not equal the speed during either real section of the motion.
misconceptions.correct_model: A gradient calculated as $\Delta\text{distance}/\Delta\text{time}$ only gives a real speed when both points lie on the same straight section of the graph. Mixing points from different sections (or from either side of a rest) gives a number with no direct physical meaning for either section.
misconceptions.remediation: Before calculating any gradient, identify and mark the single straight section the two chosen points belong to, and reject any point that falls outside it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating the shape of the graph line as a picture of the physical path travelled.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember the axes: time and distance travelled, never two position coordinates in space.
common_mistakes.why: A rising and falling line looks like a hill or a route on a map, but the vertical axis is distance travelled, not height or position in space.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling a horizontal section 'slow' instead of 'at rest'.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Calculate the gradient of the section explicitly; a horizontal section always gives exactly zero.
common_mistakes.why: 'Horizontal' can be associated with gentle or slow motion by analogy with a shallow slope, rather than with a gradient of exactly zero, which means no motion at all.

common_mistakes.mistake: Deciding which of two travellers is faster by looking at which graph is higher up at a given time.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Compare the steepness (gradient) of the two graphs at that instant, not their heights.
common_mistakes.why: A higher line suggests being 'ahead' at that moment, which describes position, not speed; speed is read from how steeply the line is rising, not from its height.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calculating a gradient using two points that do not both lie on the same straight section.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Identify the single straight section both chosen points belong to before dividing anything.
common_mistakes.why: Any two points on the graph can be substituted into the gradient formula, so it is easy to pick two convenient points without checking they both sit on the same straight stretch.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to state or check the unit of a calculated gradient.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Confirm that the vertical axis unit divided by the horizontal axis unit gives a sensible speed unit, such as m/s.
common_mistakes.why: The arithmetic of dividing two numbers feels complete on its own, so the unit that should come from dividing the axes' units is easy to leave out.

exam_notes: Before calculating any gradient, state in words which two points you are using and confirm they lie on the same straight section; this earns credit even if the final arithmetic goes wrong.
When asked to describe a graph qualitatively, use the words 'at rest', 'constant speed' and 'speeding up/slowing down' precisely — do not describe a horizontal section as any kind of moving.
A question comparing two travellers' speed at one instant is asking about gradients at that instant, not about which traveller has gone further overall.
Always give the unit of a calculated speed, and check it is consistent with the units actually printed on the two axes.

summary.big_idea: On a distance–time graph, height records how far an object has travelled so far, while the gradient of a straight section records how fast it was moving during that section — and only two points from the same section give that speed correctly.
key_points: A distance–time graph plots distance travelled (vertical) against elapsed time (horizontal); its shape is a record over time, not a map of the physical path.
A horizontal section means rest (speed zero), however large its distance coordinate is.
A straight rising section means constant speed; a steeper straight section means a greater speed.
Speed is calculated as gradient $=\Delta\text{distance}/\Delta\text{time}$, using two points that lie on the same straight section.
A curved section shows a continuously changing speed, read qualitatively as speeding up (steepening) or slowing down (flattening), without a required numerical calculation.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Height tells you how far; gradient tells you how fast — and a gradient only means something when both points you use come from the same straight section.

04_Speedtime_graphs_and_distance_travell.title: Speed–time graphs and distance travelled
04_Speedtime_graphs_and_distance_travell.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Sketch and interpret speed–time graphs for rest, constant speed, speeding up and slowing down.
Calculate distance travelled as a rectangular area under a speed–time graph for constant speed.
Calculate distance travelled as a triangle or trapezium area under a speed–time graph for constant acceleration, checking that the result has the unit of a distance (m).

prerequisites.statement: Calculate speed as distance over time (Lesson 2) and read speed from the gradient of a distance–time graph (Lesson 3).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: This lesson deliberately swaps which axis carries speed: here speed is the graph's height, not its gradient. Confusing the two roles is the single most common source of error in this lesson.

prerequisites.statement: Calculate the area of a rectangle ($\text{base}\times\text{height}$), a triangle ($\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$) and a trapezium ($\tfrac12\times(a+b)\times\text{height}$, for parallel sides $a$ and $b$).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every distance calculated in this lesson is literally one of these three area formulas applied to a graph; a learner unsure of the formulas cannot get a correct distance however well the physics is understood.

diagnostic_items.question: A rectangle has base $3$ and height $4$; a triangle has the same base and height. What is the area of each?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Rectangle: $3\times4=12$. Triangle: $\tfrac12\times3\times4=6$, exactly half the rectangle's area.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner forgets the $\tfrac12$ factor that distinguishes a triangle's area from a rectangle's with the same base and height.
The learner adds the base and height instead of multiplying them, carrying the same (wrong) operation into the $\tfrac12$ step too.
The learner doubles instead of halving, confusing the triangle's $\tfrac12$ factor with a factor of $2$.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This isolates the pure area-formula skill, especially the factor of $\tfrac12$ for a triangle, that every distance calculation in this lesson depends on.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Revise the three area formulas side by side — rectangle, triangle, trapezium — and calculate each for the same base and height before any speed–time graph is introduced.

theory_blocks.title: Why area, not height, gives distance
theory_blocks.body:
A speed–time graph plots speed (vertical axis) against elapsed time (horizontal axis). Imagine slicing the time axis into many very thin strips. During any one thin strip, the speed barely changes, so distance in that strip is well approximated by (that strip's speed) $\times$ (its tiny width) — which is exactly the area of a thin rectangle under the graph. Add up every strip's thin rectangle, and the total is the **area under the whole graph**. That is why, for a speed–time graph, distance travelled is read as [[blue:an area]], not as [[red:a height]]: height alone is only ever a speed at one instant, while the whole shaded area beneath the line is a running total of distance.

A horizontal section above zero does **not** mean rest here — it means the object is moving at a constant, nonzero speed, the mirror image of what a horizontal section meant on last lesson's distance–time graph. Only a section lying exactly on the time axis, at speed zero, means rest.

theory_blocks.title: Area under a speed–time graph is distance
theory_blocks.body:
$$\text{distance}=\text{area under the speed–time graph}$$

The units confirm this directly: speed is in $\mathrm{m/s}$ and time is in $\mathrm{s}$, so $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{m}$ — a distance, never an acceleration, however the calculation is carried out. A **rectangle** represents travel at one constant speed; a **triangle** or **trapezium** represents travel under constant acceleration, where speed itself is changing steadily.

For example, a vehicle's speed increases uniformly from $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $3\,\mathrm{s}$. The area under this rising line splits into a rectangle (the initial $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$, held for the full $3\,\mathrm{s}$) and a triangle (the extra speed gained, from $4$ up to $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$):

$$\underbrace{(4\,\mathrm{m/s})(3\,\mathrm{s})}_{\text{rectangle}=12\,\mathrm{m}}+\underbrace{\tfrac12(10-4)\,\mathrm{m/s}\times3\,\mathrm{s}}_{\text{triangle}=9\,\mathrm{m}}=21\,\mathrm{m}.$$

This can be checked by a second, independent method: for constant acceleration, the **average speed** is $(4+10)/2=7.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and distance $=7.0\,\mathrm{m/s}\times3\,\mathrm{s}=21\,\mathrm{m}$ — the same answer, found a completely different way.

assets.caption: A speed–time graph rising from $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $3\,\mathrm{s}$: the shaded rectangle (initial speed) and triangle (the increase) together give the total distance, $21\,\mathrm{m}$.
assets.purpose: Show the rectangle-plus-triangle decomposition as two distinct, separately shaded areas for a nonzero initial speed, directly countering the related idea.

theory_blocks.title: Rectangle first, then the extra triangle
theory_blocks.body:
When a speed–time graph rises from a speed that is **not zero**, always identify the rectangle first: draw (or imagine) a horizontal line at the initial speed, all the way across the time interval. Everything below that line is the rectangle. Everything between that line and the actual rising graph is the triangle. Both shapes must be calculated and **added**; the triangle alone, calculated from the *change* in speed only, leaves out every metre travelled at the starting speed itself.

Only when a graph genuinely starts from rest (speed $=0\,\mathrm{m/s}$) does the rectangle's height become zero, so that the triangle is the whole area on its own — that is a special case, not the general rule.

theory_blocks.title: Height is speed; area is distance
theory_blocks.body:
Two separate readings of the same graph must never be confused. [[blue:**Height**, read at one instant, is the object's **speed** at that instant]], in $\mathrm{m/s}$. [[orange:**Area**, built up over an interval, is the **distance** travelled during that interval]], in $\mathrm{m}$. They are different quantities, read in different ways, with different units — a height is never itself an answer to a 'how far' question, and an area is never itself an answer to a 'how fast' question.

The unit is a reliable check: if a calculated 'distance' comes out in $\mathrm{m/s}$ or $\mathrm{m/s^2}$, a height has been reported instead of an area, or a unit has been carried through a multiplication without being cancelled.

theory_blocks.title: A shape for slowing down: the trapezium
theory_blocks.body:
A speed–time graph that falls steadily, from a higher speed to a lower one, also has a straight section — and the area under it is a **trapezium**, with the two parallel sides being the initial and final speeds:

$$\text{distance}=\tfrac12(a+b)\times\text{time},$$

where $a$ and $b$ are the speeds at the start and end of the interval. A trapezium calculation and a rectangle-plus-triangle calculation are two ways of describing the same kind of straight-line change in speed; which one is quicker to use is a matter of convenience, not of different physics. The next lesson gives this steady change in speed its own name and its own number — acceleration — and calculates it directly from the gradient of exactly this kind of straight section, qualitatively anticipated here only as 'speeding up' or 'slowing down'.

keywords.definition: A graph with elapsed time on the horizontal axis and speed on the vertical axis.
The region enclosed between the graph's line and the time axis over a stated interval; equal to the distance travelled.
The area representing travel at one constant speed: base (time) $\times$ height (speed).
The area representing a steady change in speed from rest (or down to rest): $\tfrac12\times$base (time)$\times$height (speed).
The area representing a steady change in speed between two nonzero values: $\tfrac12\times(a+b)\times$time, where $a$ and $b$ are the initial and final speeds.

worked_examples.statement: **A rectangle only.** A conveyor belt moves boxes at a constant $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for $10\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the distance a box travels along the belt in this time.
reasoning: The speed–time graph for constant speed is a horizontal line, so the area beneath it over the stated interval is a single rectangle.
A rectangle's area is base (time) multiplied by height (speed); no triangle or trapezium is needed because the speed never changes.
worked_examples.interpretation: The unit check confirms it: $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{m}$, a distance, as required.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reporting $5\,\mathrm{m}$ as the answer by reading the speed-axis height alone and never multiplying by the time interval (the related idea).

worked_examples.statement: **A triangle from rest.** A trolley starts from rest and its speed increases steadily to $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $6\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the distance travelled.
reasoning: Because the trolley starts from rest, the 'rectangle' part of the area has zero height and therefore contributes nothing; the whole area under the rising line is a single triangle.
A triangle's area is $\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$, with the base the time interval and the height the final speed reached.
worked_examples.interpretation: This from-rest case is the one situation where the triangle alone really is the whole answer — only because the rectangle's height is genuinely zero, not because the rectangle can usually be skipped.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ factor and calculating $6\times12=72\,\mathrm{m}$, which is the area of the full rectangle the triangle sits inside, not the triangle itself.

worked_examples.statement: **A trapezium for slowing down.** A train's speed falls steadily from $15\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $4\,\mathrm{s}$ as it approaches a station. Calculate the distance travelled, and explain why multiplying the speed at the midpoint of the interval by the time gives the correct answer here, but would not be justified if the speed were not changing steadily.
reasoning: The area under a steadily falling straight line, between two different parallel heights, is a trapezium with parallel sides equal to the initial and final speeds.

The trapezium formula effectively uses the average of the two parallel sides, which is mathematically justified here because the speed changes at a perfectly steady rate — the same justification used for the two-method check in the rising example earlier.

Reading the speed at the midpoint of the interval ($10\,\mathrm{m/s}$) and multiplying by the whole time gives $10\times4=40\,\mathrm{m}$ here, but only because the speed falls at a steady rate, so the midpoint speed equals the average speed; if the speed changed unsteadily, one instantaneous reading could not be trusted to represent the whole interval.
worked_examples.interpretation: Using the midpoint speed happens to be justified here only because the change is perfectly steady, which is exactly what the trapezium formula's averaging already captures correctly and explicitly — it is not a shortcut that bypasses the formula, it is the same idea stated more directly.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using $15\,\mathrm{m/s}$, the larger of the two speeds, for the whole interval, giving an overestimate of $15\times4=60\,\mathrm{m}$ instead of accounting for the steady decrease.

worked_examples.statement: **Using the figure above.** A vehicle's speed increases uniformly from $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $3\,\mathrm{s}$, as shown in the figure. Calculate the total distance travelled using (a) the rectangle-plus-triangle method and (b) the average-speed method, and confirm the two methods agree.
reasoning: Method (a) splits the area into the rectangle at the initial speed and the triangle for the increase above it, and adds the two.

Method (b) instead finds the single average speed for this steady increase, $(4+10)/2$, and multiplies by the whole time, treating the motion as if it had been at that one constant average speed throughout.
The two methods must agree, because both are exact descriptions of the same straight-line area; if they disagreed, at least one calculation would contain an arithmetic error.
worked_examples.interpretation: Agreement between two independently reasoned methods is itself strong evidence that $21\,\mathrm{m}$ is correct, which is exactly why this cross-check is worth doing whenever time allows, not only as a classroom exercise.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using the triangle area alone, $9\,\mathrm{m}$, as the final answer to method (a), leaving out the rectangle for the nonzero initial speed (the related idea).

hints: Decide first whether the speed is constant or changing over the stated interval.
A constant speed gives a single rectangle: base (time) $\times$ height (speed).
Check your unit: $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}$ must simplify to $\mathrm{m}$.
guided_exercises.statement: A go-kart travels at a constant $7\,\mathrm{m/s}$ for $5\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the distance travelled.
common_errors: Reporting $7\,\mathrm{m}$ by reading only the speed-axis height.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Decide first whether the speed is constant or changing over the stated interval.

**Step 2 — Method:** A constant speed gives a single rectangle: base (time) $\times$ height (speed).

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $7\,\mathrm{m/s}\times5\,\mathrm{s}=35\,\mathrm{m}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your unit: $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}$ must simplify to $\mathrm{m}$.

hints: Check whether the motion starts from rest; if so, the rectangle's height is zero and contributes nothing.
The whole area is then a single triangle: $\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$.
Use the final speed as the triangle's height, since that is where the rise ends.
guided_exercises.statement: A skateboarder starts from rest and reaches $16\,\mathrm{m/s}$ after $8\,\mathrm{s}$ of steady acceleration down a slope. Calculate the distance travelled.
common_errors: Omitting the $\tfrac12$ factor and reporting $128\,\mathrm{m}$, the full rectangle the triangle sits inside.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Check whether the motion starts from rest; if so, the rectangle's height is zero and contributes nothing.

**Step 2 — Method:** The whole area is then a single triangle: $\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $\tfrac12\times8\,\mathrm{s}\times16\,\mathrm{m/s}=64\,\mathrm{m}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Use the final speed as the triangle's height, since that is where the rise ends.

hints: This motion does not start from rest, so there are two separate shapes to find and add: a rectangle and a triangle.
Draw (or picture) a horizontal line at the initial speed to separate the rectangle from the triangle above it.
Add the rectangle and the triangle; do not use the triangle alone.
guided_exercises.statement: A car's speed increases steadily from $3\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $9\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $4\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the total distance travelled.
common_errors: Calculating only the triangle, $\tfrac12(6)(4)=12\,\mathrm{m}$, and giving that as the final answer instead of adding the $12\,\mathrm{m}$ rectangle (the related idea).
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** This motion does not start from rest, so there are two separate shapes to find and add: a rectangle and a triangle.

**Step 2 — Method:** Draw (or picture) a horizontal line at the initial speed to separate the rectangle from the triangle above it.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Rectangle $=3\times4=12\,\mathrm{m}$; triangle $=\tfrac12(9-3)(4)=12\,\mathrm{m}$; total $=24\,\mathrm{m}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Add the rectangle and the triangle; do not use the triangle alone.

exercises.statement: A cyclist's speed increases steadily from $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $11\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $6\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the total distance travelled, using the rectangle-plus-triangle method, then check your answer using the average-speed method.
exercises.answer: Rectangle $=5\times6=30\,\mathrm{m}$; triangle $=\tfrac12(11-5)(6)=18\,\mathrm{m}$; total $=48\,\mathrm{m}$. Check: average speed $(5+11)/2=8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $8.0\times6=48\,\mathrm{m}$.

exercises.statement: A lorry's speed falls steadily from $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $8\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $6\,\mathrm{s}$ as it slows for a junction. Calculate the distance travelled while slowing down.
exercises.full_solution: This is a trapezium with parallel sides $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and $8\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and height (base) $6\,\mathrm{s}$: distance $=\tfrac12(20+8)\times6=84\,\mathrm{m}$.

exercises.statement: A student's working reads: 'Speed $=12\,\mathrm{m/s}$, time $=5\,\mathrm{s}$, so area $=12\times5=60$, giving a distance of $60\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.' Identify the one genuine error in this working (the numerical answer $60$ is correct) and explain how to fix it.
exercises.answer: The error is the unit: $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{m}$, not $\mathrm{m/s^2}$. The seconds in the time cancel with one of the 'per second' parts of the speed unit, leaving metres; the correct statement is $60\,\mathrm{m}$.

exercises.statement: A water pump delivers water at a constant flow rate of $8$ litres per minute for $5$ minutes. Using exactly the same reasoning as a speed–time area, calculate the volume of water delivered, and explain what plays the role of 'speed' and what plays the role of 'time' in this new context.
exercises.answer: Volume $=8\,\mathrm{L/min}\times5\,\mathrm{min}=40\,\mathrm{L}$. Flow rate (litres per minute) plays the role speed played before, and elapsed time plays exactly the same role it always did; the area under a (constant) flow-rate–time graph is a volume, for the same reason the area under a speed–time graph is a distance.
exercises.full_solution: The flow-rate–time graph here is a horizontal line at $8\,\mathrm{L/min}$ for $5\,\mathrm{min}$, so the area is a rectangle: $8\times5=40\,\mathrm{L}$. The unit check confirms it: $(\mathrm{L/min})\times\mathrm{min}=\mathrm{L}$, just as $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{m}$ did for distance.

exercises.statement: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to $15\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in $5\,\mathrm{s}$, travels at that steady speed for $10\,\mathrm{s}$, then brakes uniformly to rest in a further $4\,\mathrm{s}$. (a) Sketch the speed–time graph for the whole journey, labelling each axis with its quantity and unit and marking the speed and time at the end of each section. (b) State which section encloses the largest area under the graph, and say what that area represents. (c) Calculate the total distance travelled.
exercises.answer: (a) A straight line from $(0\,\mathrm{s},\,0\,\mathrm{m/s})$ to $(5\,\mathrm{s},\,15\,\mathrm{m/s})$, then a horizontal line at $15\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $(15\,\mathrm{s},\,15\,\mathrm{m/s})$, then a straight line down to $(19\,\mathrm{s},\,0\,\mathrm{m/s})$; the vertical axis is labelled 'speed (m/s)' and the horizontal axis 'time (s)'. (b) The middle section: it is a rectangle $15\,\mathrm{m/s}$ high and $10\,\mathrm{s}$ wide, giving $150\,\mathrm{m}$, which is larger than either triangle. The area represents the distance travelled during that section. (c) $\tfrac12\times5\times15=37.5\,\mathrm{m}$, plus $15\times10=150\,\mathrm{m}$, plus $\tfrac12\times4\times15=30\,\mathrm{m}$, giving $37.5+150+30=217.5\,\mathrm{m}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check on (c): the journey lasts $5+10+4=19\,\mathrm{s}$, and $217.5/19=11.4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ as an average speed, which sensibly lies between $0$ and the maximum $15\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

exam_questions.statement: A car's speed–time graph has three sections: from $t=0$ to $5\,\mathrm{s}$, constant at $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$; from $t=5\,\mathrm{s}$ to $9\,\mathrm{s}$, rising steadily from $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $14\,\mathrm{m/s}$; from $t=9\,\mathrm{s}$ to $12\,\mathrm{s}$, constant at $14\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (a) Describe each of the three sections in words. [3] (b) Calculate the distance travelled in each section separately. [3] (c) Calculate the total distance travelled over the whole $12\,\mathrm{s}$. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Section 1: constant speed. Section 2: speeding up at a steady rate. Section 3: constant speed, faster than section 1. (b) Section 1: $30\,\mathrm{m}$; section 2: $40\,\mathrm{m}$; section 3: $42\,\mathrm{m}$. (c) $112\,\mathrm{m}$.
mark_scheme: (a) section 1 correctly described as constant speed
(a) section 2 correctly described as speeding up steadily
(a) section 3 correctly described as constant speed, faster than section 1
(b) section 1: rectangle $6\times5=30\,\mathrm{m}$
(b) section 2: trapezium $\tfrac12(6+14)(4)=40\,\mathrm{m}$
(b) section 3: rectangle $14\times3=42\,\mathrm{m}$
(c) correct sum $30+40+42=112\,\mathrm{m}$

exam_questions.statement: A student calculates the area under a speed–time graph as $18\times4=72$, and states the answer as '$72\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, the acceleration'. (a) State what physical quantity this area actually represents. [1] (b) State the correct unit. [1] (c) Explain, in terms of the units of speed and time, why this unit is correct. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) Distance travelled. (b) $\mathrm{m}$. (c) Speed is in $\mathrm{m/s}$ and time is in $\mathrm{s}$, so $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{m}$: the seconds cancel, leaving a distance, not an acceleration.
mark_scheme: (a) 'distance travelled' or equivalent
(b) $\mathrm{m}$ stated
(c) correct unit-cancellation reasoning given, not just the bare assertion that it is wrong

exam_questions.statement:
The figure shows the speed–time graph of a train over $14\,\mathrm{s}$.

(a) State the speed of the train at $t=7\,\mathrm{s}$. [1]

(b) Describe the motion of the train between $t=10\,\mathrm{s}$ and $t=14\,\mathrm{s}$. [1]

(c) Calculate the distance travelled during the first $4\,\mathrm{s}$. [2]

(d) Calculate the total distance travelled in the $14\,\mathrm{s}$ shown. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$, read as the height of the horizontal section. (b) The speed falls steadily from $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so the train slows down at a steady rate until it is at rest. (c) The area under the first section is a triangle of base $4\,\mathrm{s}$ and height $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$: $\tfrac12\times4\times12=24\,\mathrm{m}$. (d) The middle section is a rectangle, $12\,\mathrm{m/s}\times6\,\mathrm{s}=72\,\mathrm{m}$, and the last section is a triangle, $\tfrac12\times4\times12=24\,\mathrm{m}$. Total $=24+72+24=120\,\mathrm{m}$.
mark_scheme: (a) Reads $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$ from the graph.
(b) States that the train slows down steadily to rest (decelerates uniformly).
(c) Identifies the area as a triangle of base $4\,\mathrm{s}$ and height $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
(c) Calculates $\tfrac12\times4\times12=24\,\mathrm{m}$, with the unit.
(d) Finds the two remaining areas: rectangle $12\times6=72\,\mathrm{m}$ and triangle $\tfrac12\times4\times12=24\,\mathrm{m}$.
(d) Adds all three areas to give $120\,\mathrm{m}$, with the unit.
