assets.purpose: Give an exam question in which speeds and times must be read off a drawn, gridded speed-time graph and converted into areas.

mcq.stem: A speed–time graph shows a horizontal line at a height of $8\,\mathrm{m/s}$, lasting $5\,\mathrm{s}$. What is the total distance travelled during this interval?

options.why_wrong: this reads the speed-axis height alone and reports it directly as a distance, without multiplying by the time interval.
this divides the speed by the time instead of multiplying them.
this adds the speed and the time instead of multiplying them.

mcq.explanation: Distance is the area under the graph: a rectangle of height $8\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and base $5\,\mathrm{s}$, giving $8\times5=40\,\mathrm{m}$.

mcq.stem: The area under a speed–time graph is calculated as $24$, from a speed in $\mathrm{m/s}$ multiplied by a time in $\mathrm{s}$. What does this area represent, and what is its correct unit?

options.why_wrong: acceleration comes from the gradient of a speed–time graph, not its area; multiplying $\mathrm{m/s}$ by $\mathrm{s}$ cancels the seconds instead of adding another 'per second'.
this is not a meaningful physical quantity for this graph, and does not match either axis being multiplied.
this is the unit of the vertical axis alone, before any multiplication by the time has been accounted for.

mcq.explanation: $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{m}$: the seconds cancel, leaving a distance in metres. The area under a speed–time graph is always a distance.

mcq.stem: A speed–time graph has a horizontal section at a constant height of $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$, above the time axis. What is happening to the object during this section?

options.why_wrong: a speed-time graph reaching exactly zero would mean rest; a horizontal section at a positive height of $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$ means the object is moving, not stationary.

options.text: It is moving at a constant $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$

options.why_wrong: a horizontal section has zero gradient, so its acceleration is zero, not $6\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$; the $6$ is a speed reading, not a gradient.

options.text: It cannot be determined without more information
options.why_wrong: a horizontal speed-time section already fully specifies the motion during that interval: a constant speed equal to the height of the line.

mcq.explanation: Height on a speed–time graph is speed at that instant, so a horizontal section at $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$ means constant motion at $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$ — the opposite of what a horizontal section means on a distance–time graph, and that is the trap this question checks.

mcq.stem: A cyclist's speed increases steadily from $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $3\,\mathrm{s}$. Which calculation correctly finds the total distance travelled?

options.why_wrong: this finds only the extra distance from the increase in speed and omits the rectangle for the nonzero initial speed of $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
this treats the whole interval as though the speed stayed at $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ throughout, ignoring that it rises to $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
this treats the whole interval as though the speed were $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ from the start, when $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ is only reached at the very end.

mcq.explanation: Since the initial speed is not zero, the total area is the rectangle at $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ plus the triangle for the rise to $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$: $12+9=21\,\mathrm{m}$.

flashcards.front: On a speed–time graph, what does the area under the graph represent, and what unit does it have?
flashcards.back: The distance travelled, in metres: $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{m}$.

flashcards.front: What are the area formulas for the three shapes used on a speed–time graph?
flashcards.back: Rectangle: base $\times$ height. Triangle: $\tfrac12\times$base$\times$height. Trapezium: $\tfrac12\times(a+b)\times$time, where $a$ and $b$ are the starting and final speeds (the parallel sides).

flashcards.front: A speed–time graph has a horizontal section well above the time axis. Is the object at rest?
flashcards.back: No. On a speed–time graph a horizontal section above zero means a constant, nonzero speed; only a section exactly on the axis (speed zero) means rest.

flashcards.front: On a distance–time graph, height gives distance and gradient gives speed. On a speed–time graph, what do height and area each give?
flashcards.back: Height gives the speed at that instant; area gives the distance travelled over that interval. The two readings are never interchangeable.

flashcards.front: A speed–time graph rises from a nonzero initial speed to a higher final speed. What two shapes must be added to find the distance?
flashcards.back: A rectangle (the initial speed held for the whole time) plus a triangle (the extra speed gained) — never the triangle alone.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The height of a speed–time graph at a given moment is the distance travelled by that moment.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: In the previous lesson's distance–time graph, height genuinely was the distance; the same reading habit is carried over to a speed–time graph, where height now means something different.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner reads a numerical value straight off the vertical (speed) axis and reports it as a distance, with no multiplication by a time at all.
misconceptions.correct_model: On a speed–time graph, height gives the speed at that instant. Distance travelled is given by the area under the graph (height multiplied by the time interval, or more generally the area of the shape formed), never by a height read alone.
misconceptions.remediation: Place a distance–time graph and a speed–time graph for the same motion side by side, and ask explicitly what a height reading means on each one.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The area under a speed–time graph has the unit $\mathrm{m/s^2}$, by analogy with speed's own unit.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Speed's unit, $\mathrm{m/s}$, is visible on the vertical axis, and a learner multiplying two numbers from the graph may carry that unit forward unchanged (giving m/s) or add a further 'per second' (giving m/s², the unit of acceleration), rather than tracking what unit the multiplication actually produces.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner's numerical area calculation is correct, but the stated unit is $\mathrm{m/s^2}$ or $\mathrm{m/s}$ rather than $\mathrm{m}$.
misconceptions.correct_model: Area under a speed–time graph multiplies a speed ($\mathrm{m/s}$) by a time ($\mathrm{s}$): $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{m}$. The seconds cancel, leaving a distance in metres, not an acceleration.
misconceptions.remediation: Carry the units through the multiplication explicitly, cancelling the seconds symbolically, every time an area is calculated, until the $\mathrm{m}$ result stops needing to be checked.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A horizontal section of a speed–time graph, like a horizontal section of a distance–time graph, means the object is at rest.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The previous lesson correctly taught that a horizontal distance–time section means rest; the rule is carried over to a speed–time graph without noticing that the vertical axis now measures something different.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a speed–time graph's horizontal section sitting above zero as 'the object has stopped'.
misconceptions.correct_model: A horizontal speed–time section above zero means the object is moving at a constant, nonzero speed — its speed is not changing, not its distance. Only a horizontal section sitting exactly on the time axis (speed $=0$) means rest.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a horizontal speed–time section at a positive height with one lying exactly on the axis, and state in words what each one means for the object's motion.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: When a speed–time graph rises from a nonzero initial speed, the distance is found from the triangle formed by the rise alone, with the initial rectangle left out.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The triangle is the visually obvious 'new' shape added by the rising section, so it is calculated on its own; the constant-speed rectangle underneath it, inherited from before the rise began, is easy to overlook because it does not look like a separate event.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: For a speed–time graph that rises from a nonzero starting speed, the learner's area calculation uses only $\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times(\text{final speed}-\text{initial speed})$, omitting the rectangle for the initial speed entirely.
misconceptions.correct_model: When the initial speed is not zero, the total distance is the rectangle (initial speed $\times$ time) **plus** the triangle for the increase, not the triangle alone. The rectangle and the triangle are two separate areas under the same straight rising line and both must be added.
misconceptions.remediation: Redraw the rising section with an explicit horizontal line at the initial speed, so the rectangle below it and the triangle above it are visually two separate shapes that must both be shaded and both be added.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading a speed-axis height and reporting it directly as a distance.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always multiply the height by a time interval (or use the full area formula) before calling a number a distance.
common_mistakes.why: A height on the graph is a single number that is easy to read off directly, which can be confused with the distance, even though distance comes from the area under the line, not a single height.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stating the unit of an area calculation as m/s or m/s².
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Cancel the units symbolically: $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{m}$, a distance.
common_mistakes.why: Because the axes are measured in m/s and s, it is easy to assume the answer keeps one of those units rather than working out what unit the multiplication actually produces.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calling a horizontal speed–time section above zero 'at rest'.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check whether the horizontal line sits on the time axis (rest) or above it (constant nonzero speed).
common_mistakes.why: A flat, horizontal line looks the same whether it sits on the time axis or above it, so it is easy to overlook that a flat line above zero means constant motion, not stillness.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using only the triangle area when a speed–time graph rises from a nonzero initial speed.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Draw the horizontal line at the initial speed first, then add the rectangle below it to the triangle above it.
common_mistakes.why: A rising line naturally suggests a triangle shape, so it is easy to overlook the rectangle of area underneath it that comes from the nonzero starting speed.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the $\tfrac12$ factor in a triangle or trapezium area.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write the full area formula out before substituting numbers, so the $\tfrac12$ is never silently dropped.
common_mistakes.why: Multiplying the two side lengths together is the first and most memorable step of a triangle's area, so the halving that comes afterward is easy to drop.

exam_notes: When a speed–time graph does not start at zero speed, always state explicitly that you are finding a rectangle and a triangle (or a trapezium) and adding them — marks are usually awarded for the method, not only the final number.
Give the unit of every calculated area as m, and be ready to justify it by cancelling $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}$ if asked.
If a question gives a two-method check (area versus average speed), show both methods rather than only the one that is quicker, since agreement between them is itself evidence the answer is correct.
Read 'horizontal' carefully: on a speed–time graph it means constant nonzero speed unless the line sits exactly on the time axis.

summary.big_idea: On a speed–time graph, height gives the speed at an instant, but distance travelled comes from the area under the graph — a rectangle for constant speed, and a triangle or trapezium whenever the speed itself is changing steadily.
key_points: Distance travelled equals the area under a speed–time graph; the unit check $(\mathrm{m/s})\times\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{m}$ confirms it is always a distance, never an acceleration.
A horizontal section above zero means constant nonzero speed, not rest — the opposite reading from a horizontal distance–time section.
Constant speed gives a rectangle; a steady change from rest gives a triangle; a steady change between two nonzero speeds gives a trapezium.
When the initial speed is not zero, the rectangle and the triangle must both be found and added — the triangle alone leaves out the distance covered at the starting speed.
A rectangle-plus-triangle area and an average-speed calculation are two independent methods for the same straight-line change in speed, and should agree.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Height is speed; area is distance — and whenever the starting speed is not zero, the area is a rectangle plus a triangle, not the triangle alone.

05_Acceleration_deceleration_and_free_fa.title: Acceleration, deceleration and free fall
05_Acceleration_deceleration_and_free_fa.subject: Physics

objectives.statement: Describe acceleration and deceleration as increasing and decreasing speed, and identify these states qualitatively from a speed–time graph.
Calculate acceleration from the change in velocity divided by the time taken, $a=\Delta v/\Delta t$, with the correct unit.
Distinguish constant from changing acceleration on a speed–time graph, and calculate the acceleration of a straight section from its gradient.
State a positive direction and use it to calculate a negative acceleration for an object decelerating while moving in one direction.
State that the acceleration of free fall near Earth's surface is approximately constant, at approximately $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, directed downward.

prerequisites.statement: Recognise velocity as speed with a direction (Lesson 2), and read the gradient of a straight graph section (Lesson 3).
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Acceleration is a rate of change of velocity, calculated by exactly the gradient technique already practised, now applied to a speed–time graph's own slope rather than a distance–time graph's.

prerequisites.statement: Subtract signed numbers correctly, including a smaller number minus a larger one, and interpret the resulting negative sign.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every deceleration in this lesson is calculated as a final velocity minus a larger initial velocity, giving a negative change; a learner unsure with signed subtraction will mishandle the sign before the physics is even applied.

diagnostic_items.question: Calculate $4-10$ and then $(4-10)\div3$.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner subtracts the smaller number from the larger one regardless of the order given, losing the negative sign both times.
The first subtraction is correct, but the division is replaced with a multiplication by $3$.
The sign is dropped in the subtraction but reappears inconsistently in the division, showing the sign is being guessed rather than tracked.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This isolates the signed-arithmetic skill — keeping a negative sign through a subtraction and then through a division — that every deceleration calculation in this lesson depends on.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Practise two more signed subtractions followed by a division by a positive number, always subtracting in the order given rather than the order that avoids a negative result.

theory_blocks.title: From 'speeding up' to a number
theory_blocks.body:
Lesson 4 described speed–time graphs qualitatively: rising meant speeding up, falling meant slowing down. This lesson puts a number on that change. Just as speed compared a distance to a time, [[blue:**acceleration**]] compares a change in velocity to a time: how many metres per second the velocity changes, per second that passes.

The everyday words 'accelerate' and 'decelerate' map directly onto this: accelerating means the speed is increasing; decelerating means the speed is decreasing. What changes in this lesson is that 'increasing' and 'decreasing' stop being only descriptions and become a single signed number with a unit.

theory_blocks.title: Acceleration: $a=\Delta v/\Delta t$
theory_blocks.body:
$$a=\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}=\frac{v-u}{t}$$

where $u$ is the initial velocity, $v$ the final velocity, and $t$ the time taken. The unit of acceleration is $\mathrm{m/s^2}$, because a velocity in $\mathrm{m/s}$ is divided by a further time in $\mathrm{s}$.

For example, a vehicle's speed increases from $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $3\,\mathrm{s}$:

$$a=\frac{10\,\mathrm{m/s}-4\,\mathrm{m/s}}{3\,\mathrm{s}}=2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

Check by substitution, rearranging to find the final velocity back again: $4\,\mathrm{m/s}+(2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(3\,\mathrm{s})=10\,\mathrm{m/s}$, which matches.

theory_blocks.title: Reading acceleration from a speed–time graph
theory_blocks.body:
On a speed–time graph, the **gradient** of a straight section is the acceleration during that section, by exactly the same reasoning that made a distance–time graph's gradient a speed: $(\mathrm{m/s})/\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

A **straight** section has constant acceleration, because its gradient does not change along its length. A **curved** section has changing acceleration: the object may be speeding up throughout, but by a different amount each second, and no single gradient value describes the whole curve — only a straight section gives one calculable acceleration.

This is a different operation from last lesson's area calculation on the same kind of graph: gradient gives acceleration; area gives distance. The two use the same two axes but are not interchangeable, and confusing them is one of the most common errors at this stage.

assets.caption: A three-section speed–time graph: a positive gradient (speeding up), a zero gradient (constant speed), and a negative gradient (slowing down), each calculated from its own straight section.
assets.purpose: Critical figure for this lesson: shows all three gradient signs on one coherent graph, kept free of any area shading so gradient and area are never visually conflated (the related idea).

theory_blocks.title: A sign convention, and what 'negative' really means
theory_blocks.body:
To use a sign for acceleration, first **state a positive direction**; every velocity and acceleration in the problem is then positive or negative relative to that one choice. If forward is positive and a car slows from $+10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $+4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in $3\,\mathrm{s}$:

$$a=\frac{4-10}{3}=-2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}.$$

The negative sign shows the acceleration points **opposite** to the chosen positive direction, and here that opposition is exactly what slows the car down.

For an object moving in the positive direction — the usual situation in exam questions — [[blue:**deceleration is a negative acceleration**]], and this is how the syllabus expects you to use it in calculations. At GCSE level, that single rule, applied to an object moving in the positive direction, is all you are required to use.

**Extension (beyond this course).** Strictly, deceleration means a decrease in speed, and a negative acceleration is not by itself a universal signal for 'slowing down'. Consider an object already moving in the negative direction, with velocity $-5\,\mathrm{m/s}$, that is then given an acceleration of $-3\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ — the same sign as its velocity. After $2\,\mathrm{s}$, its velocity is $-5+(-3)(2)=-11\,\mathrm{m/s}$: its **speed** has risen from $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $11\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The acceleration is negative and the object is **speeding up**, because the acceleration points the same way as the velocity, not the opposite way. Whether an object speeds up or slows down depends on whether acceleration and velocity point the same way (speeding up) or opposite ways (slowing down) — never on the acceleration's sign read in isolation.

**Still beyond the syllabus.** A direction change can also change velocity even while speed stays exactly the same: a car turning a corner at a perfectly constant speedometer reading is still accelerating, because its velocity's direction is continuously changing. Calculating that kind of acceleration numerically needs circular-motion mathematics that is outside this unit — the point to take now is only that acceleration is about velocity changing, and a direction change is one way for velocity to change, not only a speed change.

theory_blocks.title: Free fall
theory_blocks.body:
Near Earth's surface, an object falling under gravity alone (with air resistance small enough to ignore) accelerates at approximately

$$g\approx9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2},$$

directed downward, and this acceleration stays approximately constant throughout the fall. 'Free fall' describes an object falling freely under gravity, not an object free **of** gravity: speed increases steadily the whole time it is falling, exactly as $a=\Delta v/\Delta t$ with a constant $a$ predicts, and never stays fixed at one value.

keywords.definition: The change in velocity per unit time, $a=\Delta v/\Delta t$, unit $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
A decrease in speed. For an object moving in the positive direction, deceleration is a negative acceleration (the acceleration points opposite to the velocity).
A stated choice of positive direction, used to assign consistent signs to every velocity and acceleration in a problem.
Acceleration that does not change in value; shown as a straight section on a speed–time graph.
Motion under gravity alone, with other forces such as air resistance negligible.
The acceleration of free fall near Earth's surface, approximately $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, directed downward.

worked_examples.statement: **A straightforward acceleration.** A vehicle's speed increases from $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $3\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate its acceleration.
reasoning: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken, so first find the change: $10-4=6\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
Divide that change by the time over which it happened.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check by substitution: $4\,\mathrm{m/s}+(2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(3\,\mathrm{s})=10\,\mathrm{m/s}$, which returns the given final velocity.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing the time by the change in velocity instead of the other way round, giving $0.5\,\mathrm{s^2/m}$ — a correctly computed but meaningless quantity for this question.

worked_examples.statement: **A signed deceleration.** Taking forward as positive, a car's velocity decreases from $+10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $+4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $3\,\mathrm{s}$ as the brakes are applied. Calculate its acceleration, and state what the sign means.
reasoning: Subtract the initial velocity from the final velocity, in that order, keeping both values' signs: $4-10=-6\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
Divide by the time, keeping the negative sign through the division.

A negative result here means the acceleration points backward, opposite to the car's forward motion — and because the car is moving forward, an acceleration pointing backward is exactly what slows it down.
worked_examples.interpretation: Check by substitution: $10\,\mathrm{m/s}+(-2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(3\,\mathrm{s})=4\,\mathrm{m/s}$, which returns the given final velocity.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Reporting the acceleration as $+2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ by using the speeds' sizes only and dropping the sign that the direction convention requires.

worked_examples.statement: **When negative does not mean slower — extension, beyond this course.** Taking forward as positive, a remote-control car is already moving backward at $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ (so its velocity is $-5\,\mathrm{m/s}$), and its controller applies an acceleration of $-3\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ (also backward). Find its velocity after $2\,\mathrm{s}$, and explain whether the car has sped up or slowed down.
unknowns: Whether the car has sped up or slowed down
reasoning: Rearrange $a=(v-u)/t$ to find the final velocity: $v=u+at$.
Substitute the negative initial velocity and the negative acceleration directly, without changing either sign.
Compare the car's speed (the size of its velocity, ignoring direction) before and after, rather than comparing the signed velocities directly.
worked_examples.solution: $v=-5\,\mathrm{m/s}+(-3\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(2\,\mathrm{s})=-11\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The car's speed has increased from $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $11\,\mathrm{m/s}$: it has sped up, not slowed down.
worked_examples.interpretation: The acceleration here is negative and the car is speeding up, because the acceleration ($-3\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$) points the same way as the velocity ($-5\,\mathrm{m/s}$), not the opposite way; a negative sign on its own never settles whether an object is speeding up or slowing down.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the car must be slowing down because the acceleration is negative, without checking whether the velocity is positive or negative first (the related idea).

worked_examples.statement: **Free fall.** A stone is dropped from rest and falls freely, with air resistance negligible. Taking $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, calculate (a) its speed after $3.0\,\mathrm{s}$ of falling and (b) the distance it has fallen in that time.
reasoning: Speed after a given time of free fall from rest is $v=u+at=0+gt$, using the constant free-fall acceleration throughout.

The stone's speed–time graph from rest is a single straight line from $(0,0)$ to $(3.0,v)$, so the distance fallen is the triangular area under that line, $\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$, combining this lesson's acceleration with the previous lesson's area-as-distance rule.
worked_examples.interpretation: The stone's speed keeps rising throughout the fall (it is not constant, contrary to the related idea); after the first second it has reached $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and after the third second exactly three times that ($29.4\,\mathrm{m/s}$), exactly as a constant acceleration predicts.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating free fall as constant speed and using $v\times t$ directly for the distance, instead of recognising the speed itself is changing and using the triangular area.

hints: Find the change in speed first: final speed minus initial speed.
Divide that change by the time taken.
Check your unit: $\mathrm{m/s}$ divided by $\mathrm{s}$ gives $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
guided_exercises.statement: A cyclist's speed increases steadily from rest to $15\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $5\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the acceleration.
common_errors: Dividing $5$ by $15$ instead of $15$ by $5$, inverting the ratio.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Find the change in speed first: final speed minus initial speed.

**Step 2 — Method:** Divide that change by the time taken.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $a=(15-0)/5=3.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check your unit: $\mathrm{m/s}$ divided by $\mathrm{s}$ gives $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

hints: State the positive direction first, then assign a sign to each given velocity.
Subtract the initial velocity from the final velocity, keeping the signs.
A negative result, here, means the vehicle is decelerating, since it is moving forward throughout.
guided_exercises.statement: Taking forward as positive, a van's velocity decreases from $+20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $+5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $5\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate its acceleration.
common_errors: Reporting $+3.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ by dropping the negative sign because 'acceleration should be a positive number'.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** State the positive direction first, then assign a sign to each given velocity.

**Step 2 — Method:** Subtract the initial velocity from the final velocity, keeping the signs.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $a=(5-20)/5=-3.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** A negative result, here, means the vehicle is decelerating, since it is moving forward throughout.

hints: Rearrange $a=\Delta v/\Delta t$ to make time the subject.
Substitute the free-fall acceleration and the target speed.
Check by multiplying your answer by $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ to see if it returns the target speed.
guided_exercises.statement: A ball is dropped from rest and falls freely, with $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. How long does it take to reach a speed of $24.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$?
common_errors: Multiplying $24.5$ by $9.8$ instead of dividing, since the question has been rearranged from the usual $v=u+at$ direction.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Rearrange $a=\Delta v/\Delta t$ to make time the subject.

**Step 2 — Method:** Substitute the free-fall acceleration and the target speed.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $t=24.5/9.8=2.5\,\mathrm{s}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Check by multiplying your answer by $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ to see if it returns the target speed.

exercises.statement: A sprinter's speed increases steadily from $6\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $18\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $4\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the acceleration.
exercises.full_solution: Change in speed $=18-6=12\,\mathrm{m/s}$; acceleration $=12/4=3.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Check: $6+(3.0)(4)=18$.

exercises.statement: Taking forward as positive, a train's velocity decreases from $+14\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $+2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $3\,\mathrm{s}$ as it brakes for a station. Calculate its acceleration.
exercises.full_solution: Change in velocity $=2-14=-12\,\mathrm{m/s}$; acceleration $=-12/3=-4.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Check: $14+(-4.0)(3)=2$.

exercises.statement: Two speed–time graphs both rise from $0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $6\,\mathrm{s}$: graph P is a straight line; graph Q is a smooth curve, rising slowly at first and then more and more steeply. (a) Which graph has a constant acceleration, and which has a changing acceleration? (b) Explain why calculating $(12-0)/6=2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ correctly describes graph P throughout, but does not correctly describe graph Q at every instant, even though it gives the right value averaged over the whole $6\,\mathrm{s}$.
exercises.answer: (a) P has constant acceleration (straight line, unchanging gradient); Q has changing acceleration (curved line, gradient increasing throughout). (b) On P, every part of the line has the same gradient, so $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ is the acceleration at every instant. On Q, the gradient starts smaller than $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and ends larger than it; the single value $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ only describes the average rate over the whole interval, not the acceleration at any one particular instant within it.

exercises.statement: A skydiver falls freely (before the parachute opens), with air resistance negligible and $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Calculate her speed after $3.5\,\mathrm{s}$ of falling, starting from rest.
Taking forward as positive, a car travelling at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ brakes with a uniform deceleration of $2.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Calculate the time it takes to come to rest.
exercises.answer: A deceleration of $2.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ is an acceleration of $-2.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Rearranging $a=(v-u)/t$ gives $t=(v-u)/a=(0-20)/(-2.5)=8.0\,\mathrm{s}$.
exercises.full_solution: Check: $20\,\mathrm{m/s}+(-2.5\,\mathrm{m/s^2})(8.0\,\mathrm{s})=20-20=0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so the car is at rest after $8.0\,\mathrm{s}$.

exercises.statement: During a warm-up, a cyclist's heart rate rises steadily from $70$ to $130$ beats per minute over $2$ minutes. Calculate the rate of increase in beats per minute **per minute**, and explain why this calculation uses exactly the same reasoning as acceleration.
exercises.answer: Rate of increase $=(130-70)/2=30\,\text{beats per minute, per minute}$. This is the same reasoning as acceleration because both calculate a change in one rate (velocity, or heart rate) divided by the time over which that change happened.
exercises.full_solution: Change in heart rate $=130-70=60$ beats per minute; divided by the $2$-minute interval, the rate of increase is $60/2=30$ beats per minute, per minute. The structure $a=\Delta v/\Delta t$ and this calculation, $\Delta(\text{heart rate})/\Delta t$, are the same operation applied to two different changing quantities.

exam_questions.statement: A motorbike's speed increases steadily from $4\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $22\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $6\,\mathrm{s}$. (a) Calculate the acceleration. [2] (b) Verify your answer by substitution. [1]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $a=(22-4)/6=3.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. (b) $4+(3.0)(6)=22\,\mathrm{m/s}$, which matches the given final speed.
mark_scheme: (a) correct change in speed, $22-4=18$
(a) $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ with unit stated
(b) correct substitution check shown and matching the given final speed

exam_questions.statement: Taking forward as positive, a bus's velocity decreases from $+18\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $9\,\mathrm{s}$ as it comes to a stop. (a) Calculate its acceleration. [2] (b) State what the sign of your answer means, in terms of the direction of the acceleration. [1] (c) Explain why this situation does count as a genuine example of 'negative acceleration means slowing down', unlike the case of an already-backward-moving object given a further negative acceleration. [2]
exam_questions.answer: (a) $a=(0-18)/9=-2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. (b) The acceleration points backward, opposite to the bus's forward motion. (c) Here the velocity is positive (forward) and the acceleration is negative (backward) — opposite directions — which is exactly the condition for slowing down; this is different from an object whose velocity and acceleration share the same sign, which would instead be speeding up.
mark_scheme: (a) correct substitution $a=(0-18)/9$ (1 mark); $-2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ with negative sign and unit (1 mark)
(b) direction correctly stated as backward/opposite to motion
(c) correctly identifies that velocity and acceleration here have opposite signs
(c) correctly connects opposite signs to slowing down, distinguishing this from the same-sign (speeding up) case

challenge_questions.statement: Taking forward as positive, a car's velocity decreases steadily from $24\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ over $8\,\mathrm{s}$ when the brakes are applied. (a) Calculate the car's acceleration while braking. (b) Calculate the distance travelled while braking, using the area under the speed–time graph. (c) Verify your answer to (b) using the average-speed method instead. (d) A second car brakes from the same initial speed to rest in half the time, $4\,\mathrm{s}$. Without recalculating from scratch, state whether its braking distance is more or less than the first car's, and justify your answer using the shape of the speed–time graph rather than new numbers.
hints: Part (a) uses this lesson's gradient-as-acceleration rule; parts (b)–(c) use the previous lesson's area-as-distance rule on the same graph.
For (d), picture both graphs on the same axes, both starting at the same height and both ending at zero: the faster stop has a steeper line.
challenge_questions.answer: (a) $a=(0-24)/8=-3.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. (b) Distance $=\tfrac12\times24\times8=96\,\mathrm{m}$. (c) Average speed $=(24+0)/2=12\,\mathrm{m/s}$; distance $=12\times8=96\,\mathrm{m}$, matching (b). (d) Less: the second car's triangle has the same height ($24\,\mathrm{m/s}$) but half the base ($4\,\mathrm{s}$ instead of $8\,\mathrm{s}$), so its area — and therefore its braking distance — is half as large, $48\,\mathrm{m}$, even without a fresh calculation.
challenge_questions.full_solution: (a) Acceleration is the gradient of the straight braking section: $(0-24)/8=-3.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. (b) Distance is the triangular area under the same section: $\tfrac12\times8\,\mathrm{s}\times24\,\mathrm{m/s}=96\,\mathrm{m}$. (c) Independently, the average speed during a steady change is $(24+0)/2=12\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and distance $=12\times8=96\,\mathrm{m}$ — the two methods agree. (d) A triangle's area is $\tfrac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}$; halving the base while keeping the height the same exactly halves the area, so the second car's braking distance is $96/2=48\,\mathrm{m}$, without needing to repeat the full calculation. This also shows that, for the same starting speed, braking harder (a steeper line: $a=(0-24)/4=-6.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$) stops the car in a shorter distance.
common_errors: Calculating (a) as $+3.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ by using the speeds' sizes only, dropping the sign the forward-positive convention requires.
In (d), assuming the shorter stop must cover a greater distance because it involves 'more force' or 'more acceleration', rather than reasoning from the area of the graph.

mcq.stem: For the same straight section of a speed–time graph, what do its gradient and its area under the graph each represent?

options.text: Gradient gives distance; area gives acceleration
options.why_wrong: this reverses the two operations: gradient is a rate of change (giving acceleration), while area is an accumulation (giving distance).
area and gradient are different mathematical operations on the graph and do not give the same physical quantity.
gradient is a rate of change of speed, not an accumulation of distance; only the area represents distance.

options.text: Gradient gives acceleration; area gives distance

mcq.explanation: Gradient is $\Delta(\text{speed})/\Delta(\text{time})$, which is acceleration; area is (speed)$\times$(time) accumulated over an interval, which is distance. The same graph supports both calculations, but they are not the same operation.

mcq.stem: *Extension, beyond this course.* Taking forward as positive, a particle's velocity is $-5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ and its acceleration is $-3\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ (both backward). After $2\,\mathrm{s}$, is the particle's speed greater than or smaller than $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$?

options.text: Smaller, because a negative acceleration always means slowing down
options.why_wrong: this treats the acceleration's sign alone as decisive; here the velocity is also negative, so acceleration and velocity point the same way, which speeds the particle up, not down.

options.text: Unchanged, since both values given are negative and 'cancel out'
options.why_wrong: the two negative signs do not cancel; multiplying a negative acceleration by a positive time and adding it to a negative velocity gives an even more negative (larger-magnitude) velocity.

options.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the particle's mass
options.why_wrong: mass plays no part in this kinematics calculation; the velocity after $2\,\mathrm{s}$ follows directly from $v=u+at$.

mcq.explanation: $v=u+at=-5+(-3)(2)=-11\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so the speed rises from $5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $11\,\mathrm{m/s}$: greater. The acceleration and the velocity point the same (negative) way, so the particle speeds up despite the acceleration being negative.

mcq.stem: A speed–time graph is a smooth curve that gets steeper and steeper as time passes. What does this tell us about the acceleration?

options.why_wrong: a constant acceleration produces a straight line with unchanging gradient; a curve that keeps getting steeper has a gradient that is itself changing.
a zero acceleration produces a horizontal line (constant speed), not a rising curve.
a decreasing acceleration would make the curve rise less and less steeply over time, the opposite of what is described.

mcq.explanation: The gradient of a speed–time graph is the acceleration; a curve getting steeper over time has an increasing gradient, so the acceleration itself is increasing.

mcq.stem: Which statement about free fall near Earth's surface, with air resistance negligible, is correct?

options.text: A falling object moves at a constant speed throughout the fall
options.why_wrong: a constant acceleration means the speed is continuously increasing, not staying fixed at one value.

options.text: There is no gravity acting on an object in free fall
options.why_wrong: free fall means falling freely under gravity, with other forces such as air resistance negligible; gravity is exactly the force causing the fall, not an absent one.

options.text: A falling object accelerates at approximately $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$
A heavier falling object accelerates faster than a lighter one, with air resistance negligible
options.why_wrong: with air resistance negligible, the free-fall acceleration is approximately the same for objects of any mass; mass does not appear in the stated value of $g$.

mcq.explanation: Near Earth's surface, with air resistance negligible, any falling object accelerates at approximately $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ downward, regardless of its mass, and its speed increases steadily throughout the fall.

mcq.stem: Taking forward as positive, a cyclist moving forward slows from $12\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ in $4\,\mathrm{s}$ while braking. What is the cyclist's acceleration?

options.why_wrong: this has the correct size but the wrong sign; the cyclist is moving forward (positive) and slowing down, so the acceleration must point backward (negative).
this divides the time by the change in speed instead of the change in speed by the time, inverting the ratio.
this multiplies the speed and the time together instead of dividing the change in speed by the time.

mcq.explanation: $a=(0-12)/4=-3.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. Moving forward (positive) while slowing down requires an acceleration pointing backward (negative).

flashcards.front: What is the equation for acceleration, and what is its unit?
flashcards.back: $a=\Delta v/\Delta t=(v-u)/t$; unit $\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

flashcards.front: On a speed–time graph, what does the gradient give you, and what does the area give you?
flashcards.back: Gradient gives acceleration ($\mathrm{m/s^2}$); area gives distance travelled ($\mathrm{m}$). Different operations, different units.

flashcards.front: Is a negative acceleration always a sign that an object is slowing down?
flashcards.back: No. It slows the object down only if the acceleration points opposite to the velocity. If they point the same way (both negative, for example), the object speeds up.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between constant and changing acceleration on a speed–time graph?
flashcards.back: A straight section has constant acceleration (unchanging gradient); a curved section has changing acceleration (gradient itself changes).

flashcards.front: What is the approximate acceleration of free fall near Earth's surface, and in which direction does it act?
flashcards.back: Approximately $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, directed downward.

flashcards.front: Can an object's velocity change even while its speed stays exactly the same?
flashcards.back: Yes — if its direction changes. A car turning a corner at a constant speedometer reading is still accelerating, because velocity includes direction.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The gradient and the area of a speed–time graph are two ways of calculating the same thing.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both the previous lesson's area calculation and this lesson's gradient calculation use the same speed–time graph and the same two axes, so the two very different operations performed on it are easily blurred together.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner calculates an area when asked for acceleration, or a gradient when asked for distance, on the same speed–time graph.
misconceptions.correct_model: On a speed–time graph, the **gradient** of a straight section gives the **acceleration** ($\mathrm{m/s^2}$); the **area** under a section gives the **distance travelled** ($\mathrm{m}$). They use the same graph but are different operations, with different units and different physical meanings.
misconceptions.remediation: On one single speed–time graph, calculate both the gradient and the area of the same straight section side by side, and state in words what each one physically represents and what unit it carries.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A negative acceleration always means the object is slowing down.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: In the most familiar case (an object moving in the positive direction that then brakes), a negative acceleration does slow the object down, and this one common case is overgeneralised into a universal rule. Textbooks and the syllabus state 'deceleration is a negative acceleration' for this usual case (motion in the positive direction), and the condition about the direction of motion is easily forgotten.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner assumes an object is slowing down purely because its stated acceleration is negative, without first checking the direction of its velocity.
misconceptions.correct_model: Whether a given acceleration speeds an object up or slows it down depends on whether the acceleration points the **same** way as the velocity (speeding up) or the **opposite** way (slowing down) — not on the acceleration's sign taken alone. An object already moving in the negative direction, given a further negative acceleration, speeds up, because the acceleration and the velocity point the same way.
misconceptions.remediation: Work through a case where the moving object's velocity is already negative and the acceleration is also negative, and show explicitly that its speed increases, directly contradicting the 'negative always means slowing' rule.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A curved section of a speed–time graph still represents a constant acceleration, as long as the speed is generally increasing (or generally decreasing).
misconceptions.why_it_appears: 'Constant acceleration' is sometimes read as meaning only 'acceleration that doesn't change direction (speeding up throughout)', rather than its precise meaning of 'gradient that doesn't change value'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner calculates a single acceleration value for an entire curved section using only its first and last points, as though the whole section had one gradient.
misconceptions.correct_model: A **straight** section of a speed–time graph has constant acceleration, because its gradient does not change. A **curved** section has changing acceleration: the object may still be speeding up throughout, but by a different amount each second, so no single number correctly describes the whole curved section.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a straight rising section with a curved rising section that starts and ends at the same two points, and show that only the straight one has one well-defined acceleration value throughout.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An object in free fall moves at a constant speed, or alternatively, is not actually under the influence of gravity at all.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The everyday phrase 'free fall' suggests smooth, effortless motion, which is easily read as 'constant', and the word 'free' is sometimes misread as 'free of gravity' rather than 'free of other forces such as air resistance'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a falling object's speed as staying the same throughout the fall, or states that gravity is absent or switched off during free fall.
misconceptions.correct_model: Free fall means falling under gravity alone, with negligible air resistance; the object's speed **increases** steadily throughout, at an acceleration of approximately $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, because gravity continues to act on it the whole time it is falling.
misconceptions.remediation: Calculate the speed of a falling object at two different times using $a=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and show explicitly that the speed is different at each time, directly contradicting 'constant speed'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calculating an area when asked for acceleration, or a gradient when asked for distance, on the same speed–time graph.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Gradient gives acceleration; area gives distance. State in words which one the question is asking for before calculating.
common_mistakes.why: Both area and gradient are read from the very same graph, so it is easy to apply the wrong one of the two techniques without checking which quantity is actually being asked for.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a negative acceleration always means an object is slowing down.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Compare the signs of the velocity and the acceleration: same sign means speeding up, opposite signs mean slowing down.
common_mistakes.why: 'Negative' and 'slowing down' sound like they should go together, but whether an object speeds up or slows down depends on whether the acceleration has the same sign as the velocity or the opposite one.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using one gradient value to describe a whole curved section of a speed–time graph.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Only a straight section has one well-defined acceleration; a curved section's acceleration is changing throughout.
common_mistakes.why: A single gradient value is simple to state, which makes it tempting to apply to an entire curved section, even though a curve's steepness is different at every point along it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating free fall as motion at a constant speed.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Remember that a constant acceleration means a continuously increasing speed, never a fixed one.
common_mistakes.why: A falling object is often pictured as moving at a single, steady rate, when in fact gravity continuously speeds it up throughout the fall.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping the sign of a calculated acceleration because 'acceleration should be positive'.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Keep whatever sign the calculation produces; the sign carries real directional information relative to the stated positive direction.
common_mistakes.why: Acceleration is sometimes thought of as meaning only 'speeding up', which makes a negative result feel wrong and tempts a student to discard the sign rather than keep the directional information it carries.

exam_notes: Always state the positive direction being used before assigning a sign to any velocity or acceleration, and keep that convention consistent for the whole question.
When asked whether an object is speeding up or slowing down, compare the signs of its velocity and its acceleration; never decide from the acceleration's sign alone.
On a speed–time graph, check whether the question asks for a gradient (acceleration) or an area (distance) before calculating anything.
Give $g\approx9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ for free fall unless a question states a different value, and always state the direction (downward) when asked for it.

summary.big_idea: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, read as the gradient of a speed–time graph; its sign shows direction relative to a stated positive axis, and whether an object speeds up or slows down depends on whether that acceleration shares or opposes the direction of its velocity, not on the acceleration's sign alone.
key_points: Acceleration is $a=\Delta v/\Delta t$, with unit $\mathrm{m/s^2}$; it is the gradient of a straight speed–time section, just as speed was the gradient of a distance–time section.
A straight section has constant acceleration; a curved section has changing acceleration, with no single gradient describing it throughout.
Gradient gives acceleration; area (from the previous lesson) gives distance — the same graph, two different operations and units.
A negative acceleration slows an object down only when it points opposite to the object's velocity; when it points the same way, the object speeds up.
Free fall near Earth's surface has an approximately constant acceleration of about $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ downward, with speed increasing steadily, not staying constant.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Acceleration is Δv/Δt, read from a speed–time graph's gradient; whether it speeds an object up or slows it down depends on whether it matches or opposes the velocity's direction, never on its sign alone.

summary.big_idea: Use the key physics ideas and methods from measurement and motion accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: How many millimetres are there in (a) 1 cm (b) 4 cm (c) 0.5 cm (d) 6.7 cm (e) 1 m?
exercises.answer: (a) 10 mm (b) 40 mm (c) 5 mm (d) 67 mm (e) 1000 mm
exercises.full_solution: Since $1\text{ cm} = 10\text{ mm}$, multiply each length in cm by 10 to convert to mm: (a) $1\times10=10$ mm. (b) $4\times10=40$ mm. (c) $0.5\times10=5$ mm. (d) $6.7\times10=67$ mm. For (e), $1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}=100\times10=1000$ mm (or directly $1\text{ m}=10^3$ mm).
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, Questions (Vernier scales and micrometers), Q1

exercises.statement: What are these lengths in metres? (a) 300 cm (b) 550 cm (c) 870 cm (d) 43 cm (e) 100 mm
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, Questions (Vernier scales and micrometers), Q2

exercises.statement: (a) Write the following as powers of ten with one figure before the decimal point: 100 000, 3500, 428 000 000, 504, 27 056. (b) Write out the following in full: $10^3$, $2\times10^6$, $6.92\times10^4$, $1.34\times10^2$, $10^9$.
exercises.full_solution: (a) To write a number in standard form with one non-zero digit before the decimal point, count how many places the decimal point must move: $100\,000=1\times10^5$ (move 5 places); $3500=3.5\times10^3$ (move 3 places); $428\,000\,000=4.28\times10^8$ (move 8 places); $504=5.04\times10^2$ (move 2 places); $27\,056=2.7056\times10^4$ (move 4 places). (b) To expand a power of ten, move the decimal point that many places to the right, filling with zeros: $10^3=1000$; $2\times10^6=2\,000\,000$; $6.92\times10^4=69\,200$; $1.34\times10^2=134$; $10^9=1\,000\,000\,000$.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, Questions (Vernier scales and micrometers), Q3

exercises.statement: The pages of a book are numbered 1 to 200 and each leaf is 0.10 mm thick. If each cover is 0.20 mm thick, what is the thickness of the book?
exercises.full_solution: Each leaf (sheet of paper) is printed on both sides and carries two page numbers, so 200 numbered pages correspond to $200/2=100$ leaves. The stack of leaves is therefore $100\times0.10\text{ mm}=10.0\text{ mm}$ thick. The book also has a front and a back cover, each 0.20 mm thick, adding $2\times0.20\text{ mm}=0.40\text{ mm}$. Total thickness $=10.0+0.40=10.4$ mm.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, Questions (Vernier scales and micrometers), Q4

exercises.statement: A rectangular block measures 4.1 cm by 2.8 cm by 2.1 cm. Calculate its volume giving your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.
exercises.answer: 24 cm$^3$ (to 2 significant figures)
exercises.full_solution: Volume of a rectangular block $=$ length $\times$ breadth $\times$ height $=4.1\times2.8\times2.1=24.108\text{ cm}^3$. Each given measurement has only 2 significant figures, so the answer cannot be given to more precision than that: rounding 24.108 to 2 significant figures gives 24 cm$^3$.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, Questions (Vernier scales and micrometers), Q5

exercises.statement: How many blocks of ice cream each 10 cm $\times$ 10 cm $\times$ 4 cm can be stored in the compartment of a freezer measuring 40 cm $\times$ 40 cm $\times$ 20 cm?
exercises.answer: 80 blocks
exercises.full_solution: Along the 40 cm length, $40/10=4$ blocks fit; along the 40 cm width, $40/10=4$ blocks fit; along the 20 cm height, $20/4=5$ blocks fit (each dimension divides exactly, so there is no wasted space). The total number of blocks is $4\times4\times5=80$. This agrees with simply dividing the freezer volume by the volume of one block: $(40\times40\times20)/(10\times10\times4)=32\,000/400=80$.
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, Questions (Vernier scales and micrometers), Q6

exercises.statement:
**Extension — not examined in 0654.** this course requires only rules, measuring cylinders and clocks or digital timers (P1.1); the micrometer screw gauge is worth meeting, but it will not be asked for in the examination.

What are the readings on the micrometer screw gauges in Figures P1.9a and b? In (a) the shaft (sleeve) scale shows 0, 1 and 2 mm (the 2 mm mark is visible but not the 2.5 mm mark) and the datum line on the shaft lines up with the drum (thimble) graduation one division above the '30' mark (the drum is numbered 25, 30, 35 going upwards). In (b) the shaft scale shows 11, 12, 13 and 14 mm and the half-millimetre mark after 14 mm is visible; the datum line lines up with the drum graduation two divisions above the '45' mark.
exercises.full_solution: A micrometer reading is found by adding the whole/half-millimetre value shown on the shaft (sleeve) scale to the thimble (drum) reading, where each of the 50 divisions on the drum equals $0.05/50=0.001$ cm $=0.01$ mm (this is worked through for the example in the supplied diagram, where 2.5 mm + 33 divisions $= 0.25+0.033=0.283$ cm). (a) The last mark visible on the sleeve scale is the '2 mm' mark (the 2.5 mm mark is still hidden), so the shaft reading is $2.0$ mm. The datum line meets the drum one division above '30', i.e. at 31 divisions, adding $31\times0.01=0.31$ mm. Total $=2.0+0.31=2.31$ mm, i.e. $0.231$ cm. (b) The half-millimetre mark after 14 mm is visible, so the shaft reading is $14.5$ mm. The datum line meets the drum two divisions above '45', i.e. at 47 divisions, adding $47\times0.01=0.47$ mm. Total $=14.5+0.47=14.97$ mm, i.e. $1.497$ cm. (Read the drum carefully: count the small divisions from the nearest numbered mark to the datum line, remembering which way the numbers increase.)
exercises.source_label: Chapter P1 Motion, Questions (Vernier scales and micrometers), Q7

exercises.statement: A motorcyclist starts from rest and reaches a speed of 6 m/s after travelling with uniform acceleration for 3 s. What is his acceleration?
exercises.full_solution: Acceleration is the change of speed divided by the time taken for the change: $a=\dfrac{v-u}{t}=\dfrac{6-0}{3}=2$ m/s$^2$, since the motorcyclist starts from rest ($u=0$) and reaches $v=6$ m/s after $t=3$ s.

exercises.statement: An aircraft travelling at 600 km/h accelerates steadily at 10 km/h per second. Taking the speed of sound as 1100 km/h at the aircraft's altitude, how long will it take to reach the 'sound barrier'?
exercises.full_solution: The aircraft must increase its speed from $u=600$ km/h to $v=1100$ km/h, a change of $\Delta v=1100-600=500$ km/h. Since the acceleration is 10 km/h for every second that passes, the time needed is $t=\dfrac{\Delta v}{a}=\dfrac{500}{10}=50$ s.

exercises.statement: A vehicle moving with a uniform acceleration of 2 m/s$^2$ has a velocity of 4 m/s at a certain time. What will its velocity be (a) 1 s later, (b) 5 s later?
exercises.answer: (a) 6 m/s (b) 14 m/s
exercises.full_solution: Using $v=u+at$ with $u=4$ m/s and $a=2$ m/s$^2$: (a) after $t=1$ s, $v=4+2\times1=6$ m/s. (b) after $t=5$ s, $v=4+2\times5=14$ m/s.

exercises.statement: If a bus travelling at 20 m/s is subject to a steady deceleration of 5 m/s$^2$, how long will it take to come to rest?
exercises.answer: 4 s
exercises.full_solution: The bus slows from $u=20$ m/s to $v=0$ with deceleration (negative acceleration) of magnitude $a=5$ m/s$^2$. Using $a=\dfrac{v-u}{t}$, rearranged as $t=\dfrac{u-v}{a}=\dfrac{20-0}{5}=4$ s.

exercises.statement: The speeds of a car travelling on a straight road are given below at successive intervals of 1 second. Time/s: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Speed/(m/s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. The car travels (1) with an average velocity of 4 m/s (2) 16 m in 4 s (3) with a uniform acceleration of 2 m/s$^2$. Which statement(s) is (are) correct? A 1, 2, 3 B 1, 2 C 2, 3 D 1 E 3
exercises.answer: A (statements 1, 2 and 3 are all correct)
exercises.full_solution: The speed increases steadily by 2 m/s every second, so the motion has a uniform acceleration of $a=\dfrac{8-0}{4}=2$ m/s$^2$, confirming statement 3. Because the increase is uniform (a straight speed-time line from 0 to 8 m/s), the average velocity is the mean of the initial and final values: $\bar v=\dfrac{0+8}{2}=4$ m/s, confirming statement 1. The distance travelled is the area under the speed-time graph, a triangle of base 4 s and height 8 m/s: $\dfrac{1}{2}\times4\times8=16$ m (equivalently, $\bar v\times t=4\times4=16$ m), confirming statement 2. All three statements are correct, so the answer is A.

exercises.statement: The distance-time graph for a girl on a cycle ride is shown in the supplied diagram: starting at 1 pm with distance 0 km, the line rises to 20 km at 2 pm, continues to 30 km at 3 pm, stays flat at 30 km until 3:30 pm, rises to 45 km at 4:30 pm, stays flat at 45 km until 5:30 pm, then rises to 60 km at 6 pm. (a) How far did she travel? (b) How long did she take? (c) What was her average speed in km/h? (d) How many stops did she make? (e) How long did she stop for altogether? (f) What was her average speed excluding stops? (g) How can you tell from the shape of the graph when she travelled fastest? Over which stage did this happen?
exercises.answer: (a) 60 km (b) 5 h (c) 12 km/h (d) 2 stops (e) 1.5 h (1 h 30 min) (f) about 17.1 km/h (g) the steepest part of the graph is from 5:30 pm to 6 pm, where she rode at 30 km/h
exercises.full_solution: (a) The graph runs from 0 km (1 pm) to 60 km (6 pm), so the total distance travelled is 60 km. (b) The time axis runs from 1 pm to 6 pm, a total of 5 hours. (c) Average speed $=\dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}=\dfrac{60}{5}=12$ km/h. (d) The graph is flat (distance not changing) on two occasions: from 3 pm to 3:30 pm and from 4:30 pm to 5:30 pm, so she stopped twice. (e) The two flat sections last $0.5$ h and $1.0$ h respectively, a total stopped time of $1.5$ h (1 h 30 min). (f) Excluding stops, she was actually riding for $5-1.5=3.5$ h while still covering 60 km, so her moving average speed is $\dfrac{60}{3.5}=17.14...\approx17.1$ km/h. (g) The slope of a distance-time graph gives the speed, so the fastest travel corresponds to the steepest section of the line. Checking each riding stage: 1 pm-2 pm, $20/1=20$ km/h; 2 pm-3 pm, $10/1=10$ km/h; 3:30 pm-4:30 pm, $15/1=15$ km/h; 5:30 pm-6 pm, $15/0.5=30$ km/h. The steepest (fastest) stage is therefore the last one, from 5:30 pm to 6 pm, at 30 km/h.

exercises.statement: The graph in the supplied diagram represents the distance travelled by a car plotted against time: a straight line rises from the origin to point A at (5 s, 100 m), after which the curve bends over and flattens out, levelling off at about 120 m by roughly 6.5-7 s. (a) How far has the car travelled at the end of 5 seconds? (b) What is the speed of the car during the first 5 seconds? (c) What has happened to the car after A? (d) Draw a graph showing the speed of the car plotted against time during the first 5 seconds.
exercises.answer: (a) 100 m (b) 20 m/s (c) the car decelerates after A and comes to rest after travelling a further 20 m or so (d) a horizontal line at 20 m/s from t = 0 to t = 5 s
exercises.full_solution: (a) Reading the graph at $t=5$ s (point A) gives a distance of 100 m. (b) From $t=0$ to $t=5$ s the graph is a straight line through the origin, so the car's speed is constant over that period and equals the gradient: $v=\dfrac{100\text{ m}}{5\text{ s}}=20$ m/s. (c) After A the graph is no longer a straight line: its slope (the speed) steadily decreases until the curve becomes horizontal at about 120 m, so after A the car decelerates and eventually comes to rest, having travelled a further $120-100=20$ m or so after passing A. (d) Since the speed is constant at 20 m/s for the whole of the first 5 seconds (part b), the speed-time graph for $0\le t\le5$ s is simply a horizontal straight line at $v=20$ m/s.

exercises.statement: the supplied diagram shows an incomplete speed-time graph for a boy running a distance of 100 m: speed rises in a straight line from 0 at t = 0 to 5.0 m/s at t = 4 s, then stays constant at 5.0 m/s from t = 4 s onward (the graph as drawn only extends to t = 14 s). (a) What is his acceleration during the first 4 seconds? (b) How far does the boy travel during i the first 4 seconds, ii the next 9 seconds? (c) Copy and complete the graph showing clearly at what time he has covered the distance of 100 m. Assume his speed remains constant at the value shown by the horizontal portion of the graph.
exercises.answer: (a) 1.25 m/s$^2$ (b) i 10 m ii 45 m (so 55 m is covered by t = 13 s) (c) he reaches 100 m at t = 22 s
exercises.full_solution: (a) Over the first 4 s the speed rises uniformly from 0 to 5.0 m/s, so the acceleration is $a=\dfrac{5.0-0}{4}=1.25$ m/s$^2$. (b) i The distance in the first 4 s is the area of the triangle under the speed-time graph: $\tfrac12\times4\times5.0=10$ m. ii From $t=4$ s to $t=13$ s (the 'next 9 seconds') the speed is constant at 5.0 m/s, so the distance covered is $5.0\times9=45$ m. By $t=13$ s the boy has therefore covered $10+45=55$ m in total. (c) He still needs $100-55=45$ m, which at the constant speed of 5.0 m/s takes a further $45/5.0=9$ s. So the horizontal line of the graph must be extended (kept at 5.0 m/s) until $t=13+9=22$ s, at which point the total area under the graph (and hence the total distance run) reaches 100 m.

exercises.statement: The approximate speed-time graph for a car on a 5-hour journey is shown in the supplied diagram (there is a very quick driver change midway to prevent driving fatigue!): speed rises from 0 at O (t = 0 h) to 80 km/h at A (t = 1 h), stays constant at 80 km/h from A to B (t = 3 h), rises to 100 km/h at C (t = 3.5 h), stays constant at 100 km/h from C to D (t = 4.5 h), then falls to 0 at E (t = 5 h). (a) State in which of the regions OA, AB, BC, CD, DE the car is i accelerating, ii decelerating, iii travelling with uniform speed. (b) Calculate the value of the acceleration, deceleration or constant speed in each region. (c) What is the distance travelled over each region? (d) What is the total distance travelled? (e) Calculate the average speed for the whole journey.
exercises.answer: (a) i accelerating: OA and BC; ii decelerating: DE; iii uniform speed: AB and CD. (b) OA: 80 km/h$^2$; AB: 80 km/h (constant); BC: 40 km/h$^2$; CD: 100 km/h (constant); DE: -200 km/h$^2$ (i.e. a deceleration of 200 km/h$^2$). (c) OA: 40 km; AB: 160 km; BC: 45 km; CD: 100 km; DE: 25 km. (d) 370 km. (e) 74 km/h.
exercises.full_solution: The speed-time graph is read off at each labelled point: O(0 h, 0 km/h), A(1 h, 80 km/h), B(3 h, 80 km/h), C(3.5 h, 100 km/h), D(4.5 h, 100 km/h), E(5 h, 0 km/h). (a) The speed rises in OA and BC (accelerating), is level in AB and CD (uniform speed), and falls in DE (decelerating). (b) Acceleration is the gradient of each section: OA, $(80-0)/(1-0)=80$ km/h$^2$; AB, 0 (speed constant at 80 km/h); BC, $(100-80)/(3.5-3)=40$ km/h$^2$; CD, 0 (speed constant at 100 km/h); DE, $(0-100)/(5-4.5)=-200$ km/h$^2$, i.e. a deceleration of 200 km/h$^2$. (c) Distance is the area under the graph in each region: OA is a triangle, $\tfrac12\times1\times80=40$ km; AB is a rectangle, $2\times80=160$ km; BC is a trapezium, $\tfrac12(80+100)\times0.5=45$ km; CD is a rectangle, $1\times100=100$ km; DE is a triangle, $\tfrac12\times0.5\times100=25$ km. (d) Total distance $=40+160+45+100+25=370$ km. (e) Average speed $=\dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}=\dfrac{370}{5}=74$ km/h.

exercises.statement: The distance-time graph for a motorcyclist moving at constant speed is shown in the supplied diagram: it is a single straight line from the origin (0 s, 0 m) to (30 s, 600 m). (a) Describe the motion. (b) How far does the motorbike move in 30 seconds? (c) Calculate the speed.
exercises.answer: (a) The graph is a straight line through the origin, so the motorbike moves with constant (uniform) velocity for the full 30 s. (b) 600 m (c) 20 m/s
exercises.full_solution: (a) Because the distance-time graph is a single straight line (constant gradient) all the way from $t=0$, the motorbike's speed does not change during the 30 s shown: it travels with constant (uniform) velocity throughout. (b) Reading the graph at $t=30$ s gives a distance of 600 m. (c) Speed is the gradient of the distance-time graph: $v=\dfrac{600\text{ m}}{30\text{ s}}=20$ m/s.
